labradorite.opening: Hold a strand up and turn it slowly. One bead goes flat gray, the next throws a sheet of blue across its whole face, and a third gives you a thin edge of gold before it closes again. Faceted labradorite does this bead by bead, so no two strands look alike. The body color runs gray to near black, which is why people reach for it: a neutral that lights up when the wrist moves.
labradorite.history: Labradorite was first identified in Labrador, Canada, and takes its name from that peninsula. The geological type area is Paul's Island, near the town of Nain. It is a plagioclase feldspar, sitting between albite and anorthite, and it forms in mafic igneous rocks such as basalt, gabbro and norite. In anorthosite it can be the most abundant mineral in the rock, and it is one of the more common plagioclase varieties. It has since been reported in Poland, Norway, Finland, China, Australia, Slovakia, the United States and Madagascar. Most of the rough cut for beads today comes out of Madagascar. As a gem it is usually cut en cabochon, with a rounded convex surface. The beads on our strands are faceted instead. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
labradorite.lore: The color play has a name of its own, labradorescence, borrowed from the stone that made it famous. What makes it happen is ordinary enough: light reflecting off thin twin layers inside a gray to black body. What tradition made of it is less ordinary. Because the flash appears and disappears as the bead turns, labradorite has long been called a stone of transformation, and that is how crystal tradition still describes it. The observation behind the belief is one any maker makes at the bench: the light sits inside the stone all the time, and the angle is what decides whether you can see it.
labradorite.uses: This is the gray-with-fire neutral, and it works hardest next to silver and in boho stringing. Faceted pears and daggers hang well from an ear wire, swinging and catching light from more angles than a still bead does. Rectangles suit statement necklaces, where the broad faces let a full sheet of blue show. Beads around 7x13mm keep to a scale that will string a whole necklace, while pieces closer to 20x37mm want to be the only thing in the design. Blue across most of the bead is the usual look; the strands with stronger flash add gold, green and purple alongside it. We list ten strands.
labradorite.care: Labradorite is 6 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale with perfect cleavage, so a hard knock can split a bead and big nuggets tend to chip along their edges. Keep it to earrings, pendants and loose necklaces rather than tight bracelets. Clean with warm soapy water only, never in an ultrasonic or steam cleaner.
labradorite.tagline: Gray until it turns, then blue across the whole face.

emerald.opening: Small green points on the strand, not one big statement. The faceted rondelles are shaded: one end of the run sits pale as new grass, the other goes deep, and the color holds green in daylight instead of sliding toward gray. Turn a bead to the window. Inside is the mossy garden, the jardin, which is how you know you are looking at beryl. A little of that green does a lot next to yellow gold.
emerald.history: Emerald is beryl that grew with chromium and vanadium in it. That trace chemistry marks the whole difference between an aquamarine and this green. The ancients took their emeralds from Upper Egypt, where the deposit is said to have been worked as early as 2000 BC, and mining there ran intermittently from around 500 BCE onward, continuing through Cleopatra's reign. Its name arrived by a long road from the Greek smaragdos. Pliny the Elder described the stone in his Natural History in the first century AD and settled the matter in three words: nothing greens greener. Colombia later became the classic source. The material that reaches us as beads comes mostly from Zambia and Brazil, with lower-grade Colombian and Indian stone as well. Zambian color at bead prices is a matter of size. Small pieces. Emerald all the same.
emerald.lore: In crystal tradition, emerald is the gem of spring and of beginnings. People have long tied it to rebirth and to foresight. The Jewel of Kings, one old name has it. Pliny recorded a belief among early lapidaries that no green did more for tired eyes, and wrote of that green as a comfort people had known long before his own century. It is the birthstone for May, and the gem given for the twentieth and thirty-fifth wedding anniversaries. Famous stones carry that history forward. Among them is the 75.47-carat Hooker Emerald, worn by Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II, the last sultan of the Ottoman Empire.
emerald.uses: Shaded faceted rondelles at 2.5 to 3mm are the workhorse. They suit long single strands and wrapped bracelets, and layering where one green line sits under a chain. Figure 10 to 15 carats per 8 inches. A strand goes further than it looks. Smooth hearts and pears near 7mm get bought for gifts, often for a May birthday. Green next to yellow gold needs no help from anything else. We list ten strands, cut in Jaipur, India and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
emerald.care: Warm water, mild soap, a soft cloth. Emerald sits at 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale. It is also brittle, and nearly every stone carries internal fractures. Treat it like something softer than it is. Keep it away from ultrasonic cleaners and steam. No jewelry dip. No hot dashboards.
emerald.tagline: Green first. Everything else comes after.
emerald.judge: Draft B packs in more concrete, source-grounded detail (hardness/brittleness in care, specific historical dates, clearer shape/size pairing) and avoids the repetitive phrasing that weakens Draft A's voice. (a 34, b 38)

sapphire.opening: Hold a strand of 3mm rondelles to a window. The color moves bead to bead: ink blue in one, slate gray in the next, one almost violet. Facets this small give back light in hard points rather than a broad shine. On the pink strands the color sits somewhere between raspberry and dusty rose. Makers reach for these because it is the same mineral that goes into a ring stone, only cut small and sold by the inch.
sapphire.history: Sapphire is corundum: aluminum oxide, with traces of iron and titanium. Every color but red carries the name. Red corundum is ruby. The word arrived through the Latin sapphirus, from the Greek sappheiros, a name of Semitic origin that once pointed at lapis lazuli. For centuries the stone decorated the robes of royalty and clergy, and its blue became the standard against which other blue gems, from topaz to tanzanite, get measured. Romance came back into the story in 1981, when Prince Charles gave a blue sapphire engagement ring to Lady Diana Spencer; she wore it until her death in 1997. Bead grades come out of Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Tanzania including the Umba valley and Songea, and India. Cutting happens in Jaipur. We choose the strands one at a time here in Cupertino, California.
sapphire.lore: Sapphire is the September birthstone and the gem of the fifth anniversary. Wisdom and loyalty attach to it in tradition. Older writing links it to nobility and truth, puts sincerity and faithfulness on the same list, and holds that the stone stands for fidelity and for the soul. For centuries people believed a sapphire worn on the body guarded its owner against poison and fraud, which is part of why it sat in the rings of kings and bishops. Star sapphires drew legends of their own. None of it is fact. It is still why a blue bead gets picked for an engagement piece, or for a gift marking a long marriage.
sapphire.uses: Micro-faceted rondelles at 2 to 3mm are the volume item, wire wrapped onto gold-fill chain for bridal work and September birthdays. Pink pear briolettes make quick earrings. Nuggets come organic cut rather than faceted and sit softer next to gold. Ninety strands are listed. Blue leads, and pink across a dozen lots. Green and yellow. Umba banded and confetti, and Umba orange with olive and lavender and honey. Songea in gray and black, in brown and mauve. Sold by the 8 inch and the 16 inch, about 20 carats per 8 inches at 3mm. A stronger strand throws color back at every facet instead of reading flat and dark.
sapphire.care: At Mohs 9 sapphire takes daily wear, and an ultrasonic gives it no trouble. Care is mostly about what sits beside it in the bead box. Store these strands apart from softer stones. A sapphire bead will scratch a quartz bead, so give it a pouch of its own.
sapphire.tagline: Hardness 9, cut small: the strand a granddaughter still wears.

ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.opening: Hold a strand of white Welo to a window and the beads read like frosted glass, until one turns and a patch of green lifts out of it, then orange, then blue. The crystal beads go further: bodies close to colorless, with the color floating inside, so you look through the bead and into the flash at the same time. No two match, even on one strand. Makers reach for them because each bead behaves differently in the light of a room.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.history: Opal from Ethiopia began entering the gem and jewelry market in 1994, after a small find put the country on the opal map. Material from Mezezo has been known since the mid-1990s for its brown play-of-color, called chocolate opal. The find that changed the trade came in 2008, near the village of Wegel Tena in Wollo province in the north, in volcanic rock. That deposit runs mostly white, with some brown, some fire opal, and some colorless crystal opal, and its play-of-color is often very vivid. Gemologists describe it as opal-CT, with inclusions of pyrite, barium-manganese oxides and native carbon, and some pieces show interpenetrating digit patterns. Another important discovery followed in 2013. Welo is now the opal most often seen in the trade, and beads are one of the most popular things cut from it. Ours are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.lore: Opal carried meaning in ancient Rome, where it stood for love and hope, and the Roman name opalus was used as a word for precious stone in general. In 75 AD Pliny wrote that some opals hold a play of color equal to the deepest and richest colors of painters, while others seem to hold the flaming fire of burning sulphur or the bright blaze of burning oil. Later collectors gave great opals names of their own: Pandora, Light of the World, Empress. Writers have compared the stone to volcanoes, galaxies and fireworks. Opal is the October birthstone, and tradition ties it to hope.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.uses: Drops are the piece to start with. A pear at 7x9mm hangs well on an earring wire or a fine chain, and one bead is enough for a pendant. Nuggets keep the organic edge people want in boho and bridal work, and their uneven faces catch color from more directions. Marquise beads run long here, out to 10x40mm, which suits a single center drop rather than a repeated pattern. Pair any of them with gold fill or oxidized silver. A brighter bead flashes green, orange and blue from several angles instead of one narrow tilt. Opal is light: figure about 20 carats per 8 inches at 4mm. We list three strands.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.care: Welo is hydrophane and drinks water. Take it off for showers, swimming and lotion. If a bead clouds or goes glassy, set it somewhere dry and leave it a few days to come back. Keep it away from ultrasonic cleaners and heat, and store it apart from harder stones.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.tagline: White and crystal opal, each bead flashing its own way.
ethiopian-welo-opal-white-and-crystal.judge: Draft B packs in more concrete, sourced detail (opal-CT, digit patterns, exact sizes/weights) and keeps lore tightly tied to documented tradition, while Draft A drifts into invented, unsourced belief claims about opal's effects. (a 35, b 41)

tanzanite.opening: Held to a window, a tanzanite bead does two things at once. Turn it one way and it reads blue. Turn it again and violet rises through the facets, with a bronze cast at some angles that you catch only when the strand swings. Along a strand the color runs uneven. One bead pale lavender, the next deeper. That unevenness is part of the appeal, and makers reach for it when they want a violet-blue that will not be mistaken for amethyst.
tanzanite.history: Tanzanite is blue-violet zoisite, a calcium aluminum silicate. It comes from one place on earth: the Merelani Hills near Arusha in northern Tanzania, within sight of Mount Kilimanjaro. The common account of the discovery has Maasai herders finding transparent blue crystals weathering out of the ground in 1967 while they tended livestock. They told a prospector named Manuel d'Souza. He registered four mining claims and believed for a time that he had found a new sapphire deposit. Careful gemological study identified the crystals instead as a transparent variety of zoisite. Tiffany & Co. introduced the material to the trade as tanzanite, after the country, rather than selling it as blue zoisite. A 122.70-carat stone sits in the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India. We pick them strand by strand here in Cupertino, California.
tanzanite.lore: Tanzanite is a recent arrival, so it carries none of the layered legend that older stones gathered over centuries. What it has instead is custom. Young custom. It was added to the December birthstone list in 2002, and jewelers who mark birth months have used it that way ever since, which makes it a frequent gift for a December birthday. Maasai tradition links the color blue with new birth, and people who sell and give the stone often repeat that association when they speak about it. In crystal tradition the stone is linked with calm, and it is said to steady a wearer facing something new. All of this is belief, passed along with the stone rather than proven by it.
tanzanite.uses: Faceted rondelles in 3 to 4mm are the workhorse. They sit between metal spacers as accents, and they take a wire wrap cleanly. Small beads also stretch a little material across a long necklace. At 4mm, figure roughly 35 carats in an 8 inch strand. Plan before you cut wire. Teardrops at 3x5mm hang as earring pairs, or as a single center drop on a fine chain, which is how most December birthday pieces get made here. A stronger strand shows saturated blue-violet with a clear purple flash when turned. A weaker one stays light and cloudy, closer to gray-blue.
tanzanite.care: Tanzanite is Mohs 6 to 7 and has one direction of perfect cleavage, so a sharp knock can split a bead. Keep it to necklaces and earrings rather than bracelets or rings. Wipe with a soft damp cloth. Skip the ultrasonic cleaner and steam, and keep the beads away from sudden changes in temperature.
tanzanite.tagline: One hill in Tanzania, blue one way and violet the next.

australian-opal-gray-body.opening: A gray body opal bead looks quiet until you turn it. The ground is the color of wet slate, and against it the play-of-color reads clearly, flashing across the surface and shifting as the light moves. Some beads carry more color than others, and a good strand is mostly the ones that do. Makers reach for the gray because the color shows in ordinary daylight, not only under a lamp. Hold a strand up to a window and the flash is there without coaxing.
australian-opal-gray-body.history: Opal forms from silica dissolved in water, laid down slowly by circulating groundwater. In Australia that process began about 140 million years ago, when an inland sea covered much of the continent, and the result is plain in the numbers: Australian opal accounts for about 95 percent of the world's supply. People mined opal long before that trade existed, in places such as Kenya and Hungary as far back as 4,000 BCE, and Rome knew the stone as opalus, a word it also used to mean precious stone. Australia has been the primary source since the 1880s, and the town of Coober Pedy produces more opal than anywhere else. Bead material is still spoken of by field. Coober Pedy, Mintabie and Andamooka give the light and gray bodies; Lightning Ridge gives the dark. Precious opal is silica holding about 6 percent water, which is why it behaves unlike any quartz.
australian-opal-gray-body.lore: In ancient Rome the stone stood for love and hope. In 75 AD Pliny wrote that some opals carry such a play within them that they equal the deepest and richest colors of painters, while others simulate the flaming fire of burning sulphur. Later writers compared opals to volcanoes, galaxies and fireworks, and admirers gave the great stones poetic names: Pandora, Light of the World, Empress. Crystal tradition still ties opal to hope, and people have long worn it in that spirit, as a stone of good expectation. It is the birthstone for October. Australia named opal its national gemstone in 1993.
australian-opal-gray-body.uses: Heishi discs are the workhorse here, and they go to boho and layered-necklace makers. Faceted rondelles suit wire-wrappers. Smooth ovals go out to people who want one bead to carry a pendant. We carry all three with gray body and play-of-color, sold by the 8 inch and the 16 inch strand, and an 8 inch length usually runs 20 to 30 carats. On a strong strand most beads flash rather than reading as plain gray potch, and the side of each heishi disc should be solid opal, with no straight seam or dark backing. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen one at a time in Cupertino, California.
australian-opal-gray-body.care: This is the most forgiving opal, non-hydrophane and stable, with a hardness of 5.5 to 6.5. Warm water and a soft cloth are enough. Keep it away from ultrasonic cleaners, dry heat and sudden temperature swings. There are no water rules to remember, so you can wear it and forget it is on.
australian-opal-gray-body.tagline: Gray ground, daylight color, no water rules to remember.
australian-opal-gray-body.judge: Draft B sticks closer to the sourced facts and keeps lore clearly framed as tradition, while Draft A adds an unsupported, vaguely mystical claim about the stone carrying "that country's open light." (a 32, b 40)

tourmaline.opening: A multi tourmaline strand reads like a paint box. Pink beside mint, then a deep sea blue, then a green so saturated it looks wet. Turn the strand in the light and the tones shift, because tourmaline is darker along the length of the crystal than across it, so a bead can hold two moods depending on how it was oriented at the wheel. Watermelon beads show the family trait plainly: a pink core grading out to a green rind. People reach for it when one color is not enough.
tourmaline.history: The name comes from the Sinhalese toramalli, stone with mixed colors. Dutch merchants used the word for the water-worn pebbles miners found in the gem gravels of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, and the Dutch East India Company carried those Ceylonese stones to Europe in quantity to satisfy a demand for gems and curiosities. Meanwhile, somewhere in Brazil in the 1500s, a Spanish conquistador washed the dirt off a green crystal and took it for emerald. The 1554 expedition of Francisco Spinoza is credited with that so-called Brazilian emerald, and the confusion lasted until scientists recognized tourmaline as a distinct mineral species in the 1800s. The old mistake still lingers in trade names for green alkali tourmaline. Our bead grades come from Afghanistan, Nigeria, Brazil, Mozambique and Madagascar. The strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and we choose them one by one in Cupertino, California.
tourmaline.lore: October has two birthstones, opal and tourmaline, and tourmaline is also the gem of the eighth anniversary. An Egyptian legend, carried as tradition rather than fact, has the stone passing through a rainbow. Ancient mystics are said to have believed that a gem with a shade for every mood could inspire artistic expression, and crystal folklore still treats a multi strand as a stone for creative work. Because tourmaline comes in more colors and color combinations than any other mineral group, people have long picked a bead by its hue and let that choice carry meaning. All of it is belief, passed along with the beads themselves.
tourmaline.uses: Faceted multi rondelles at 3mm and 4mm are the workhorse. Knotted on silk or strung plain, they put eleven colors in a necklace without any one bead shouting. At 3mm, count on roughly 17 carats in an 8 inch strand, useful when you are planning a run of bracelets. Watermelon slices work as focals, and wire-wrappers like them because the pink core and green rind already do the design work. Crystal sticks are the mineral as it grew, good beside a clasp or strung short and plain. We list twelve strands, including watermelon along with single-color pink and green.
tourmaline.care: Tourmaline sits at 7 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale and has no cleavage, so it takes daily wear well, bracelets included. Clean with warm water, mild soap and a soft brush. Keep included beads and slices out of ultrasonic and steam cleaners, and store strands away from harder stones.
tourmaline.tagline: Eleven colors, one mineral, one strand.

chocolate-and-brown-ethiopian-opal.opening: On the strand the color runs from milk chocolate to tan to a red-brown that reads almost like cinnamon in daylight. Then a bead turns. Green comes up through the brown, or orange, or a quick line of blue along one facet. The body color is dark enough that the flash looks lit from inside rather than laid on top. Faceted, the fire arrives in small bright pieces. People reach for these when white opal feels too cool for the rest of their work.
chocolate-and-brown-ethiopian-opal.history: Precious opal from Ethiopia reached the gem trade in 1994, after a small find in the Shewa area near Mezezo. That is where the brown bodies come from. By the mid-1990s Mezezo was known for chocolate opal with play-of-color, and the Smithsonian keeps an 8.86 carat chocolate cabochon from that deposit. A second discovery, much larger, came in 2008 near the town of Wegel Tena in Wollo Province. That material is mostly white, though it also yields brown opal and fire opal and colorless crystal opal. The trade name Welo comes from the province. Wollo material is now what most people mean by Ethiopian opal. Gemstones played little part in Ethiopia's long history until these last few decades. Opal is what changed that. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, then chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
chocolate-and-brown-ethiopian-opal.lore: In ancient Rome opal stood for love and hope, and the Roman name opalus was used as a word for precious stone in general. In 75 AD Pliny wrote that some opals held a play equal to the deepest and richest colors of painters, while others seemed to carry the flaming fire of burning sulphur or the blaze of burning oil. He marveled that one gem could hold the red of ruby along with so much else. Later writers compared opals to volcanoes and to fireworks. Great stones were given poetic names: Pandora, Light of the World, Empress. By long custom opal is the October birthstone, and that custom follows the brown bodies as much as the white.
chocolate-and-brown-ethiopian-opal.uses: Designers working in copper and bronze, or in oxidized silver, tend to find this the opal that agrees with their metal. It turns up often in autumn collections. A 7x13mm pear hangs as a single drop, with room for the flash to move as it swings. Seven millimeter trilliants set a rhythm in a row along a collar. Heishi gives a denser, steadier line of color for a bracelet. We keep eleven strands at the moment, faceted, along with smooth rondelles sold as full strands. On the strongest strands the play crosses the whole bead as it turns rather than blinking in pinpoints.
chocolate-and-brown-ethiopian-opal.care: Opal sits at 5.5 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale, so store it apart from harder beads. Keep it dry. No lotion or hand cream on the beads, and put a piece on last after you dress. Never an ultrasonic cleaner, never heat. A soft dry cloth is all it needs, and a drawer out of the sun.

swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.opening: Two blues from the same mineral. Sky blue is the paler one, a soft wash close to aquamarine, cool and quiet with no gray in it. Swiss blue is bright and electric, the blue of a pool light, and it holds that color even in small sizes. On a strand of faceted rondelles the stones are clear enough to see straight through, so the light comes back off the facet edges in short flashes rather than glowing from within.
swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.history: Topaz is aluminum silicate with fluorine and hydroxyl, Al2SiO4(F,OH)2, and it sits at 8 on the Mohs scale. The name and its variants were used for yellowish gems for at least two thousand years, and before the twentieth century nearly any transparent yellow, brown, or orange stone was called topaz. Modern gemology narrowed the term to one species, defined chemically and physically. The color range turns out to be unusually wide: brown, blue, green, yellow, orange, red, pink, purple, and colorless, which is plentiful. Blue crystals grown by nature are very rare; one specimen from Zimbabwe measures 4.6 by 4.2 by 3.1 centimeters. Before 1970 most topaz in low to moderate price jewelry was yellow to brown. Blue is now the most popular topaz color in the jewelry market, sold from pale light tones through deep, darker blues. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.lore: Topaz has long been linked in folklore to love and to astrology. Because so many of the old stones called topaz were yellow, some people believed the gem could draw gold to its owner. In crystal tradition blue topaz is associated with calm, a settling of the thoughts at the end of a loud day, and that is belief passed along rather than fact. Precious topaz is a birthstone for November. Blue topaz is one of the modern birthstones for December, and it is the gem given for a fourth wedding anniversary. Sellers of birthstone pieces keep both blues on hand through the fall and into winter.
swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.uses: Faceted rondelles at 4mm are the workhorse, about 35 carats to an eight inch strand, and they go to just about everyone: makers turning out affordable something blue pieces for weddings, and sellers who stock by birth month. Nuggets go to designers building a single statement piece, and those strands run 80 to 120 carats. We carry both blues, plus carved melons. A stronger strand shows even color from end to end and crisp, unrounded facet junctions. Sky blue for the bride, Swiss blue for the bridesmaids, is an easy way to build a wedding set.
swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.care: Wash with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry well with a soft cloth. Avoid hard knocks against other stones in a bead box or a bowl. Keep drilled beads out of ultrasonic cleaners, since the vibration works on the drill hole. The color is stable and will not fade with wear.
swiss-blue-and-sky-blue-topaz.tagline: One mineral, two blues: pale sky and bright Swiss.

london-blue-topaz.opening: On the strand, London blue reads darker than a photograph suggests. Deep steel blue with a green undertone. Closer to inky teal than to sky. Hold one up to a window and the color glows through. Set it on a bench and it goes almost navy in the hollows between the facets. Most are clean enough that nothing interrupts the color, so what you see is depth and the sharp meeting of facet edges. People reach for it when they want saturated blue that still reads as a gemstone.
london-blue-topaz.history: Topaz is aluminum fluorosilicate, Al2SiO4(F,OH)2. Hardness 8, with one direction of perfect cleavage. The name comes from a Sanskrit word for fire, and versions of it have been attached to yellowish gems for at least two thousand years. Before the twentieth century, any transparent yellow, brown or orange stone might be sold as topaz, and many early gem traders had no way to tell one material from another. Modern gemology drew the line and made topaz a distinct species. In low to moderate price jewelry, topaz stayed largely yellow to brown until about 1970. Blue is the rare case in nature. One crystal on record came out of Zimbabwe, measuring 4.6 by 4.2 by 3.1 centimeters. London blue names a color rather than a place: a deep tone, darker than Swiss blue. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, then chosen one at a time in Cupertino, California.
london-blue-topaz.lore: Wealth is the association topaz has carried longest. Older writing on the stone reaches further, into health and love and astrology, and lists of gem meanings still repeat those pairings. Blue topaz has its own reputation in crystal tradition. It is said to be the calm one of the family, and people have long believed that keeping one close settles the mind. All of that is tradition. Topaz is the birthstone for November. Blue topaz is listed for December as well, in company with blue zircon, tanzanite and turquoise, and older custom names it the gem of the fourth wedding anniversary.
london-blue-topaz.uses: We carry faceted pears and marquise, and they go into earrings most often, hung so the beads swing and catch light from behind. Carved melons work as focals, wide enough to hold the color at the center of a piece. At 3mm and 4mm, the beads carry a line of blue without weight. Figure roughly 20 carats per 8 inches at 3mm and 35 at 4mm. Pair them with plain gold or with a warm stone. The strongest strands stay inky under lamp light instead of thinning toward aqua. Topaz runs about a third heavier than quartz, so a matched strand feels dense in the hand.
london-blue-topaz.care: At 8 on the Mohs scale, topaz shrugs off scratches. Cleavage is the weak point. There is one direction of it, and it is perfect, so a sharp knock against a bench edge can split a bead. Keep the strand out of ultrasonic cleaners. Warm water and mild soap, a soft cloth after. Sunlight does not touch the color.
london-blue-topaz.tagline: Inky teal that keeps its depth under lamp light.
london-blue-topaz.judge: Draft B works in the concrete carat-per-strand figures and cutting-location detail the pack specifies while staying tighter to sourced facts, whereas Draft A pads the care section with unsupported advice and skips the specific quantities. (a 36, b 43)

natural-zircon.opening: Hold a strand of natural zircon up to a window and the colors sort themselves out: honey, cognac, red-brown, a few beads leaning olive. The beads are small and they are heavy, heavier than they look, and they throw more fire than any other brown stone we handle. Look through a loupe at a faceted rondelle and the far facet edges appear doubled, two lines where you expect one. That doubling is how the stone signs its name.
natural-zircon.history: Zircon is a zirconium silicate that turns up as a minor mineral in granite, in gneiss, and in the sediments washed out of them, which makes it common in the ground and uncommon on a bead strand. The brown and multicolor material we buy comes from Tanzania, Sri Lanka and Madagascar. People have cut it as a gem for nearly two thousand years. Many scholars think the name comes from the Arabic word zarkun. Colorless zircon has refraction and fire close enough to diamond that the two were confused for centuries, and in the early 1900s it was used widely as a diamond simulant, a role later taken by more convincing look-alikes. That history is why the name still says imitation to some buyers. Zircon from Australia holds a different record: at 4.4 billion years, it is the oldest known mineral on earth. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
natural-zircon.lore: In the Middle Ages, zircon was thought to bring on sound sleep, to drive away evil spirits, and to promote riches, honor and wisdom. Some held that it reduced temptation and sharpened the mind. Crystal writers today call it a Stone of Virtue and describe it as grounding, and the old association with prosperity and untroubled rest still follows it. Zircon is a birthstone for December, sharing the month with turquoise and tanzanite, which is how many people first come to ask for it by name. All of this is belief and tradition rather than fact, and we pass it along in that spirit.
natural-zircon.uses: Faceted rondelles at 3mm are the ones makers reach for most, strung plain on a fine chain or knotted for a short necklace, catching light at every turn of the head. Pear briolettes make quick earrings. Smooth ovals read calmer, with less flash per bead. Warm brown against gold is the pairing we see most often. Plan for weight: figure about 26 carats per 8 inches at 3mm, and 48 at 4mm. We stock rondelles from 3 to 4mm, plus briolettes and ovals, in brown and multi, by the 8 inch and the 16 inch.
natural-zircon.care: Zircon runs 6 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale and its facet edges are brittle, so it makes a poor bracelet stone. Keep it in necklaces and earrings, where it takes fewer knocks. Wash with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry it. Never an ultrasonic.
natural-zircon.tagline: The real December stone, and heavier than it looks.
natural-zircon.judge: Draft B sticks closer to the sourced lore and history, includes an explicit tradition-not-fact disclaimer, and pairs that fidelity with more concrete, less marketing-flavored detail than Draft A, which invents unsupported lore embellishments. (a 36, b 42)

sphene.opening: On the strand, sphene reads olive at first, the color of a bay leaf held up to a window. Tilt it under a lamp and the smooth ovals throw small sparks of orange and green from somewhere inside. Its dispersion measures 0.051 against diamond's 0.044, so the fire is real, and it shows even on a rounded polish with no facets to help it. Most people who pick up the tray cannot name the stone. That is usually why they keep holding it.
sphene.history: Titanite forms as an accessory mineral in granitic and calcium-rich metamorphic rocks. It is a minor ore of titanium and a minor gemstone, and gem-quality material comes from Madagascar, Skardu in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Brazil and Mexico. The older name comes from the Ancient Greek word for wedge, after the shape of the crystals. In 1982 the International Mineralogical Association adopted titanite and discredited sphene. Geologists and mineralogists switched almost at once, while gemologists and gem dealers kept sphene, especially in Europe and especially for transparent and faceted material. Larger crystals tend to carry inclusions and flaws, so clean gems stay small and mostly reach collectors rather than production jewelry. Laboratories have grown titanite for work in geology, pigments and radioactive waste disposal, but no synthetic version is sold as a jewelry stone. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
sphene.lore: The lore attached to sphene is recent, written by modern crystal authors rather than handed down through generations. In that tradition it is described as a stone of clear thinking, something people like to keep on the desk or around the neck while they are studying, sorting out a problem or deciding what to say. Because of the way it flashes, it is said to lift a flat mood and to encourage plain speech and a little courage. Some who work with crystals also hold that it draws out creative energy that has gone quiet. All of this is belief and custom rather than anything measured, and it travels with the stone the way stories do.
sphene.uses: This is a focal stone, not a full necklace. Smooth ovals around 6x8mm hang well from a simple bail on a fine chain, and 8x10mm gives you a single dramatic drop with room for the fire to show. Pairs make good earrings, where the beads swing and catch lamplight. Sphene is strongly pleochroic, so the color shifts as the bead turns. Greener, more transparent beads throw the strongest flash, and under a loupe you will see very strong doubling and a near-adamantine luster. Peridot is the closest color match, harder and oilier looking, with none of the fire. We carry smooth ovals from a single 950 carat lot, roughly sixteen to twenty eight-inch strands.
sphene.care: Keep sphene to pendants and earrings. At 5 to 5.5 on the Mohs scale, with cleavage, it does not belong in a bracelet or a ring. Skip the ultrasonic cleaner and the steamer. Store the strand alone in a soft pouch, since other beads will scratch it. The rough is small and fragile to begin with.
sphene.tagline: More fire than diamond, and few can name it.
sphene.judge: Draft B delivers more vivid, concrete detail (crystal shape origin, IMA timeline, synthetic-use note, styling specifics) while still framing lore as tradition, giving it an edge in specificity and voice despite a couple of unsourced styling additions. (a 39, b 41)

kunzite.opening: On the strand it reads pale pink with a violet undertone, closer to the inside of a shell than to candy. Turn one bead in daylight and the color moves: pink, then lilac, then nearly colorless. The color is thin, which is why size matters here. A 4mm rondelle reads as glass, while a 10mm melon holds enough pink to carry a necklace on its own. Makers reach for it when they want scale, big soft-colored beads that still look like gemstone.
kunzite.history: Kunzite is the pink to lilac variety of spodumene, a lithium aluminum silicate that takes its color from traces of manganese. Spodumene itself was first described in 1800 from Uto, in Sodermanland, Sweden, by the Brazilian naturalist Jose Bonifacio de Andrada e Silva, who named it from the Greek word for burnt to ashes after the dull gray look of material refined for industry. The pink kind came much later. It was found in the pegmatites of Pala, in San Diego County, California, in 1902, and recognized as a distinct variety of spodumene by the American gemologist George Frederick Kunz, whose name it carries. San Diego County is still an important source. Bead-grade rough now comes from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Brazil and Madagascar. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
kunzite.lore: Some kunzite pales after long hours in bright light, drifting toward colorless, and that habit gave it the nickname evening stone. Certain traditions count it as an alternate birthstone for February. In modern crystal folklore it is described as a stone of emotional healing, and people who keep such stones tend to file it with the soft and quiet ones rather than the guardians. It is said to suit anyone going through a tender stretch. All of this is belief and custom, carried hand to hand and repeated because people like thinking that way, not a claim about what the stone does for anyone.
kunzite.uses: This is a stone for blush palettes and bridal work, where pale pink needs to hold its own next to white metal and pearl. Because the color is soft, size carries it: carved melons at 8 and 10mm give a focal run real presence, while tubes suit bar pendants and short vertical drops. Smooth nuggets work as spacers between richer stones. A stronger strand shows the color shift plainly as you rotate a bead; a weaker one stays one flat tint. We carry melons, nuggets, tubes and ovals, and melons come in heavy, so plan clasps and knots for the weight.
kunzite.care: Keep it out of direct sun and off windowsills, since the color can fade with long exposure. No ultrasonic, no steam, no hot water, no sitting under halogen lamps. Cleavage runs perfectly in two directions at 6.5 to 7 hardness, so skip bracelets and store the strand away from light.
kunzite.tagline: Pink that needs ten millimeters to show itself.
kunzite.judge: Draft B pulls in more sourced specifics (spodumene's 1800 Sweden origin, the evening-stone reasoning, February alternate birthstone) and avoids the small invented styling details found in Draft A. (a 36, b 44)

chrome-diopside.opening: A strand of 3mm chrome diopside rondelles looks like a line of wet grass held up to a window. The green comes from chromium, the same element that colors emerald, and the small facets throw a quick, hard spark. Size matters more here than with most stones. Above about 5mm the color darkens toward near black, so the little beads are the ones that stay lit. Makers reach for them when they want green that reads as gem rather than as rock.
chrome-diopside.history: Diopside is a common pyroxene, a calcium magnesium silicate that forms in igneous and metamorphic rocks in many countries. The chromium-bearing green kind turns up near kimberlite pipes. Occurrences are reported in Canada, South Africa, Brazil and Russia, and in the United States in the serpentinite belt of northern California, in the kimberlite of the Colorado-Wyoming State Line district, and at Iron Mountain, Wyoming. For a long time diopside was a collector's stone, faceted in small numbers and seldom seen in commercial jewelry. That changed with one source: the Inagli deposit in Yakutia, in eastern Siberia, worked only through the short summer, which supplies nearly all the material cut for jewelry. In 1988 this new green gem from Russia began to be seen in the jewelry industry. Sellers sometimes borrow emerald for the name. It is not emerald, and the borrowed name misleads.
chrome-diopside.lore: Chrome diopside carries no inheritance of old legend. It came out of Siberia within living memory, so it missed the centuries of lapidary writing and folk custom that gathered around older green stones. Whatever is said about it now belongs to modern crystal practice, where writers group it with the green stones and lean on the reputation of emerald, whose color it shares and whose coloring element it holds. All of that is tradition, held and passed along, rather than fact. There is field lore of a plainer kind as well. Prospectors read scattered grains of chrome diopside in the ground as an indicator that diamonds may lie nearby, and they have dug on that sign for years.
chrome-diopside.uses: We carry it in one form, faceted rondelles at 3mm, cut in Jaipur and picked strand by strand here in Cupertino. Figure roughly 18 carats on an 8 inch strand. The way it sells best is as an accent: short runs of the green set between freshwater pearls, where the flash of the facets breaks up all that soft white. It suits earrings, short necklaces and pendant stations, and it sits well against silver, which keeps the green cool. On the brightest strands the beads read grass green rather than forest, stay clear to the eye, and show doubled facet edges under a loupe.
chrome-diopside.care: Chrome diopside is Mohs 5 to 6 with two directions of cleavage, so keep it to earrings and necklaces rather than bracelets or rings, where knocks are constant. No ultrasonic cleaner and no steam. Wipe with a soft cloth. Store the strand apart from harder beads so nothing scratches the facets.
chrome-diopside.tagline: Grass green from Siberia, cut small so it glows.
chrome-diopside.judge: Draft B weaves in more concrete fact-pack details (the 18ct/8in weight, specific mineral localities, the 1988 trade date) and ties the lore explicitly to its recent, modern origin, giving it an edge in specificity and lore handling while matching Draft A elsewhere. (a 41, b 44)

aquamarine.opening: Strung in a line, aquamarine shows a clear, even blue that reads as water. Faceted rondelles throw quick, bright glints; smooth ovals carry the color in steady blocks. Milky strands glow soft. Mossy strands hold fine green threads and flecks that hint at the rock it grew in. On the neck the hue stays light, not heavy, and plays well with silver or gold. Makers reach for it for March gifts, bridal work, and pieces that want a calm blue.
aquamarine.history: Aquamarine is blue to green-blue beryl colored by iron. On the Mohs scale it measures 7.5 to 8. It mainly forms in granite pegmatites and often grows as large, clean crystals suited to sizable cuts and carvings. The name comes from Latin: aqua for water and marina for of the sea; English use of aquamarine is recorded in 1677. Today bead rough comes from Brazil, Nigeria, Mozambique, and Pakistan. Aquamarine is the same mineral species as emerald, but in a different hue. Top stones are known for high clarity with transparent blue to slightly greenish blue color, a look that has long worked well for beads and pendants. Its durability and steady color have kept it in regular jewelry use.
aquamarine.lore: In crystal tradition, aquamarine is March's birthstone and a sailor's stone, said to calm waves and help keep seafarers safe. It is also said to brighten marriages and bring happiness to partners. In Western lore its sea color links it to safe travel over water. Wider beryl lore holds that it brings protection in battle or litigation, makes the wearer amiable and unconquerable, and quickens the intellect. Modern custom names aquamarine as the 19th wedding anniversary gem. These are long-held beliefs about meaning, passed along with the stone.
aquamarine.uses: Makers reach for faceted rondelles and pear briolettes for bridal and March-birthday pieces; milky and mossy strands lean into beach and boho work. We carry clean blue rondelles in 4 to 6 mm, pear briolettes, and smooth ovals, with multi-beryl mixes as well. Moss is aquamarine with its geology left in. When choosing, an even medium blue with no gray reads best, and moss is loveliest when inclusions are spread evenly. Rondelles and briolettes sell best. Blue topaz feels heavier and more saturated; glass shows round bubbles. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino.
aquamarine.care: Aquamarine is daily-wear durable. Clean with warm soapy water. Ultrasonic cleaning is safe for most pieces, but avoid it on moss material with inclusions. When in doubt about mossy strands, stick to warm soapy water.
aquamarine.judge: Draft A folds in more of the pack's concrete details (look-alikes, judging criteria, 'sell best,' the moss talking point) while staying just as faithful and well-structured as Draft B. (a 40, b 38)

morganite.opening: Hold a strand up to a window and the color reads like the blush on a peach, pale pink leaning warm. It is quiet color, never loud. What makes people reach for it is the clarity: small glassy windows between the facets, light going in and coming back out again. Set it next to rose quartz and the difference is plain. The quartz is pinker and hazy all through. Morganite is beryl, first cousin to aquamarine, and it wears like one.
morganite.history: Morganite is a beryl, the same mineral family as emerald and aquamarine, and its pink to orange-pink comes from traces of manganese. When a new source of rose beryl was found in Madagascar in 1910, George Frederick Kunz proposed the name morganite, after the financier J. P. Morgan, himself a keen collector of gems. Tiffany & Co. brought the stone to the American market. It grows in lithia pegmatites as squat tabular crystals, sometimes banded blue near the base and peach at the terminations, and those pockets can be generous: miners in Brazil have found crystals as heavy as 22 pounds. Most morganite on the market still comes from the pegmatite mines of Minas Gerais. The bead rough we see is Brazilian, Mozambican and Nigerian. Since 2010 it has become the second most popular colored center stone for engagement rings, after sapphire.
morganite.lore: In crystal tradition morganite is spoken of as a stone of compassion, and that one word carries most of what folklore attaches to it. People who keep such stones describe it as gentle rather than forceful, and many prefer to wear it against the skin through the day rather than leave it in a drawer. Much of the belief seems to follow the color itself, which is soft and warm and does not push. As gem lore goes, this is a young tradition. The stone was not named until 1910, so the stories told about it have had only a century to gather, and they are still mostly about kindness.
morganite.uses: We carry morganite at 6mm in two cuts, smooth tubes and faceted rondelles, both good sizes for bracelets that get worn every day. The tubes sit flat and give a clean line of color; the rondelles catch more light at the facet edges. Both like rose gold, and they read well in bridal and blush palettes, or as a step up from rose quartz for someone who wants the same soft pink with more life in it. A stronger strand shows soft peach-pink with real transparency, glassy luster, and crisp facets rather than a milky look. Strands come by the 16 inches, or by the 8.
morganite.care: Morganite is hard enough for daily wear, between 7.5 and 8 on the Mohs scale. Wash it in warm soapy water with a soft brush; an ultrasonic is usually safe. The one real caution is light. Long hours in strong sun can pale the color, so store your pieces in a drawer or pouch.
morganite.tagline: Pale peach beryl, clear where rose quartz stays cloudy.
morganite.judge: Draft B matches the fact pack's retail and hardness details more fully and reads in a plainer, less ornamented voice while staying just as faithful and well-structured as Draft A. (a 37, b 39)

amethyst.opening: On the strand, amethyst settles into medium to dark purple, bead after bead. Tip it to a window and a red or blue flash shows. The color reads from across the room and still feels easy up close. Small faceted rondelles make tight, even lines. Pears and hearts throw a clean sparkle in earrings. Dark African material looks almost inky indoors, then opens in bright light.
amethyst.history: Amethyst is quartz, Mohs 7, worn for more than two millennia. A necklace with amethyst beads dates to 2000 BCE, and the center stone bears an inscription in a South Arabian script from the 8th century BCE. Ancient Greeks wore amethyst and carved drinking vessels from it, and Romans linked it to Bacchus. It was as expensive as ruby and emerald until large deposits in Brazil were found in the 19th century. Today Brazil and Uruguay supply much of the volume, while Zambia is known for darker African material. Zambian material can show more inclusions, though in small rondelles they disappear to the eye. We cut our beads in Jaipur, India, and choose them strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
amethyst.lore: In crystal tradition, amethyst is the sobriety stone. The name comes from the Greek amethystos, "not drunk." Legends tie it to Dionysus, called Bacchus by the Romans, and people long said it kept the mind clear and quick in battle and in business. Greeks wore it and carved drinking vessels, saying it would ward off drunkenness. It is also the birthstone for February, and by custom the gem for the 6th and 17th wedding anniversaries. One old note says the patron of romantic love wore an amethyst ring carved with Cupid.
amethyst.uses: We keep it working in everyday pieces. Small faceted rondelles build bracelet stacks and mixed strands with steady color. Pears make clean, bright earrings; hearts add a friendly center to a pendant. We stock 3x5mm rondelles for tight spacing and 9x15mm pears when a single drop is enough. A stronger red or blue flash shows in the top color; hold it to the light to see it. Dark African material is cut small to keep the eye on color. Our strands are faceted in Jaipur and chosen here in Cupertino.
amethyst.care: Amethyst wears well every day. Clean with warm soapy water and a soft cloth. An ultrasonic is usually safe, but skip steam. Keep it out of direct sun, since strong light can fade the color over time.
amethyst.tagline: Purple quartz with an old story
amethyst.judge: Draft A stays tightly anchored to the fact pack and keeps a plain, even voice, while Draft B adds a few unsupported specifics (strand color variation, metal-pairing rationale, extra cleaning steps) and drifts toward marketing phrasing. (a 40, b 36)

pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.opening: On a strand, Rose de France shows a clear lilac that reads cool and airy, while pink amethyst leans blush with a hint of lavender. Facets catch small flashes rather than bold fire, so the line feels calm and bright. The color is meant to be soft. Makers reach for these beads when they want pastel light without opacity, a clean sparkle that sits easily beside pearl and moonstone, and a quartz that holds its own in everyday wear.
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.history: Amethyst is the purple variety of quartz. Rose de France is a trade name for pale lilac to lavender amethyst, mainly from Brazil. Pink amethyst is a newer name for pinkish-lavender quartz from Patagonia, Argentina, its color tinted by tiny hematite inclusions. Amethyst has been used in personal adornment for over 2000 years. Ancient Greeks wore amethyst and carved drinking vessels from it in the belief that it protected against drunkenness. The word amethyst comes from Greek amethystos, "not intoxicated." Both of these pale lines keep quartz durability at hardness 7 and show well with crisp faceting. Rose de France is real amethyst; the name describes the shade. Pink amethyst is from one Patagonian deposit. In these stones the color is meant to be soft; even tone and clarity let the cut read clean.
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.lore: In crystal tradition, pale amethyst shades are linked with calm and clear thought. Because both stones are amethyst in composition, many people fold them into February birthstone customs by association. Ancient Greeks wore amethyst and carved cups from it, saying the stone would keep a drinker sober; the name comes from Greek amethystos, meaning not intoxicated. Some modern crystal lore extends those ideas to Rose de France and pink amethyst, noting their gentle tones. People have long believed these colors can support calm and a clear head as softer expressions of amethyst.
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.uses: We carry faceted step-cut nuggets and rondelles, plus oval beads, cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen one strand at a time in Cupertino, California. Makers use the nuggets for a single station or a full necklace; rondelles sit neatly as spacers that still catch light. We stock 10x13 mm. These stones sit well with rose quartz, moonstone, and pearl for bridal and other pastel work. When choosing, look for even lilac across a strand, eye-clean material, and crisp facets. Pink amethyst often shows a faint red-brown hematite dusting under a loupe.
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.care: Quartz at hardness 7 is everyday durable. For cleaning, use warm soapy water, rinse well, and dry with a soft cloth; an ultrasonic is usually safe. Avoid strong sun during wear and storage to protect the pale color.
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.tagline: Pale amethyst in lilac and rose, cut in Jaipur
pink-amethyst-and-rose-de-france.judge: Draft A sticks closer to the fact pack, while Draft B invents an unsupported historical narrative about pale amethyst being treated as 'leftovers' before taste changed. (a 39, b 39)

prasiolite.opening: On the strand, prasiolite shows a soft mint, pale and slightly yellowish green, with clear light passing through. It reads quiet and fresh and lifts open, airy designs. We reach for strands that are clean yet natural, not too even. Vivid or bottle green sets off alarms. Lookalikes often appear overly perfect; glass may show round bubbles. In hand, the beads feel cool and easy. That gentle color is why makers come back to it.
prasiolite.history: Prasiolite is a green, transparent variety of quartz. The color has been linked to Fe2+ in the crystal structure. Natural prasiolite is rare. It was first reported in the early 19th century in Lower Silesia, Poland, with only a few other deposits noted. Material from Brazil has supplied the trade, and prasiolite is commonly cut into faceted stones for jewelry. Many people have not heard the name, which is one reason it is less common in store cases. The word prasiolite comes from Greek for leek green, and the stone has also been called green amethyst and vermarine. Like other quartz, it sits at Mohs 7, so it stands up well in daily wear. Today you will see it as matched bead strands and as center stones, carrying a pale, yellowish green that suits light metal and open settings.
prasiolite.lore: In crystal tradition, prasiolite borrows amethyst's calm. People who work with stones often keep the link in mind through the older trade name green amethyst. The thought is simple: if amethyst is held for quiet and ease, this clear green quartz is said to carry a similar steadiness with a lighter touch. The gentle, leaf-toned color is part of the association in lore, and many place it beside amethyst in meaning. Stories in the trade lean on that kinship more than on separate claims for prasiolite itself. As always with folklore, these are held as beliefs about mood and presence rather than promises.
prasiolite.uses: Prasiolite suits spring palettes and peridot-without-the-price designs. We carry faceted long ovals and carved melons, cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino. Long ovals make balanced station necklaces and quiet line earrings. Melons give a single bold note on a chain or at the collarbone. We like two sizes for most work: 7x13 mm for stations and 11 mm when a bead needs presence. Faceting shows a calm, pale green that stays clear in simple layouts and leaves room for light.
prasiolite.care: Quartz at Mohs 7 is everyday durable. Use warm soapy water and a soft cloth. An ultrasonic cleaner is usually safe. Skip steam. Keep the strand away from a torch or high heat at the bench. Store it separate from softer stones to avoid scuffs.

citrine-and-lemon-quartz.opening: On the strand, Madeira citrine reads like cider held up to a lamp, orange-brown and warm at the core, with the little facet flats catching light along the drill line. Lemon quartz sits at the other end of the family: a cool, clean yellow, closer to the peel than the juice. People reach for both because the color carries across a room without turning heavy, and because quartz at Mohs 7 takes daily wear without much thought.
citrine-and-lemon-quartz.history: Quartz has been worked into jewelry for thousands of years. Egyptians gathered striped agates from the shore and carried them as talismans, the Greeks carved ornaments from rock crystal, and Roman pontiffs wore rings set with large purple amethysts. Citrine belongs to that same mineral family, the yellow to brownish orange end of it. The name comes from the Latin citrus, the citron tree, by way of the French citrin and citron, for lemon. Egyptian jewelers used the stone early. Later, before modern gemology sorted one yellow gem from another, its tawny color was often confused with topaz, and it was sometimes sold under names borrowed from topaz. Pieces from the Victorian era still surface. Natural citrine is uncommon, yet color, durability and a fair price have made it the best-selling yellow to orange gem. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
citrine-and-lemon-quartz.lore: In crystal tradition, citrine carries a second name: the merchant's stone. The name points toward trade and prosperity, and those who keep the tradition like to have a piece somewhere near their work rather than shut away in a drawer. What the stone is said to bring the wearer follows from that, a sense of good fortune in dealings and exchange. Along with topaz, citrine is a birthstone for November, which is why so much of it turns up in autumn gifts. It is also the gem given to mark a thirteenth wedding anniversary. Believe as much or as little of that as you like; the color is reason enough to wear it.
citrine-and-lemon-quartz.uses: We carry faceted rondelles in Madeira and shaded citrine and in lemon quartz, small at 3 to 4mm, which suit spacing between larger stones or a continuous strand knotted onto silk. The pear briolettes are the ones makers hang: one at the center of a chain, or a graduated row across a collar. Larger drops at 9x15mm read well against oxidized silver and against warm gold both. Look for saturated orange-brown with no muddy zones in Madeira, and a clean, cool yellow in lemon quartz. A stronger strand throws an even flash from every bead rather than one or two.
citrine-and-lemon-quartz.care: Citrine and lemon quartz are hard enough for everyday wear. Wash with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry before storing. Ultrasonic cleaning is usually safe. Keep lemon quartz out of long hours of direct sun, since prolonged light can pull the yellow down over time.

ametrine.opening: On a strand, ametrine shows clean planes of violet and honey that switch as the bead turns. One face reads amethyst; the next shows citrine. The meeting line can look straight as a window edge. Makers reach for it when they want two tones without two strands. Purple and gold share the same bead. One crystal, two moods. Autumn palettes sit easily with saturated jewel tones. The look stays crisp and orderly.
ametrine.history: Ametrine is bicolor quartz with zones of amethyst purple and citrine yellow sharing a single transparent crystal. The name joins amethyst with citrine, and the gem is also called amethyst-citrine, trystine, golden amethyst, and, in trade, bolivianite. Quartz occurs worldwide, and people have used it in jewelry for thousands of years. By contrast, ametrine is a relative newcomer to the trade, available in small quantities for just a few decades. Its only commercial source is the Anahí mine in Bolivia, which yields the material in commercial amounts. In this quartz, iron in two oxidation states produces the purple and yellow sectors, often divided by a crisp boundary. It is considered rare, with a finite supply reported from that single source. The striking contrast of two hues in one crystal carried it into modern jewelry.
ametrine.lore: In crystal tradition, ametrine is spoken of for two hues sharing one clear stone. People have long believed that it blends amethyst's calm with citrine's optimism for balance. It is said to steady attention and support clear intention. Writers in the crystal world often use the name amethyst-citrine, and they point to the visible line where purple meets yellow as a sign. Turn it a little and the leading color flips. A small reminder, in that telling, to pause and choose with care. Some also speak of mental clarity and gentle confidence, held in one gem.
ametrine.uses: We use ametrine when a design needs two tones from one strand. The switch from purple to gold shows best in faceted step-cut nuggets, and in smooth ovals for softer lines. Clear boundary. Strong contrast. Strands with muddy tan-purple read quieter. It suits autumn palettes and deeper jewel tones. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India. We choose them strand by strand in Cupertino, California. One well chosen strand can set contrast through a bracelet or a simple necklace, the color flipping as each bead turns.
ametrine.care: Ametrine, Mohs 7, handles everyday wear. Warm, soapy water works well for routine cleaning, and ultrasonic cleaning is usually safe. Avoid heat during wear and storage. Keep finished pieces away from high temperatures, and store them in a dry place out of direct heat.

rose-quartz.opening: Hold a strand of rose quartz to a window and the light does not pass straight through. It slows down and spreads, so each bead glows from the inside rather than sparkling on the surface. The pink is soft, closer to the inside of a shell than to a candy color, and the faceted edges catch small flat highlights. That haze is the mineral itself, microscopic pink fibers related to dumortierite, not a flaw in the cutting. People reach for it because the color is honest and easy to wear.
rose-quartz.history: Rose quartz grows in the quartz cores of pegmatites, formed at 400 to 700 degrees Celsius, and it comes out of the ground in massive lumps rather than clean crystals. Most of what reaches the bead market is from Brazil, Madagascar, South Africa, and India. It is an old material in jewelry. Beads dating to 7000 BC have been found in the area once known as Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, and the Assyrians were crafting rose quartz jewelry around 800 to 600 BC. The Romans used it as a seal to signify ownership. Along with the Assyrians, they may have been among the first to work this stone. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, faceted to wake up a stone that is naturally quiet, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
rose-quartz.lore: Rose quartz has been carried for a very long time as a stone of love, and in crystal tradition it is the one people reach for when the love in question is for themselves. It is said to soften how a person speaks to themselves, and to hold a steady, forgiving kind of warmth rather than a bright one. The ancient Egyptians are said to have used it as a talisman believed to hold off the signs of age. Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians all regarded quartz as a stone with power in it. By custom, rose quartz marks the fifth wedding anniversary.
rose-quartz.uses: The 3 to 4mm faceted rondelles do double duty. Run a full strand for a bracelet that reads as one soft line of pink, or scatter them between larger stones as spacers where you want a break in color without a break in sparkle. They also stand up to bulk stringing for gift lines without pushing the price up. We cut rose quartz faceted in hearts, pears, and ovals as well, in sizes from 5x7mm up to 9x15mm. We list seven strands at a time, sold by the 16 inch strand and by the half. Buy three and match the pinks; an even medium pink with a soft glow looks far stronger than a chalky white one.
rose-quartz.care: At 7 on the Mohs scale, rose quartz handles daily wear. Wash it in warm soapy water with a soft brush, and an ultrasonic cleaner is fine. The one thing to watch is sunlight. Years on a sunny windowsill or a car dashboard will pull the pink out of it, so store finished pieces in a drawer or a pouch.
rose-quartz.tagline: The honest pink, hazy by nature.

crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.opening: On a strand, clear quartz looks like water that has been cut and held still. Each faceted bead throws small white sparks, and the drill hole shows as a bright line through the middle. Rutilated quartz is the same clear stone with fine gold needles running through it, some in loose parallel bundles, some crossing at angles. Turn a bead and the needles catch light one at a time. Pick one up and it stays cold in your palm. Glass warms.
crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.history: Rock crystal comes out of Brazil, Madagascar and India. Golden rutilated quartz is nearly all Brazilian. The needles inside it are rutile, the most abundant of the three natural forms of titanium dioxide, which grows as slender brilliant crystals, often enclosed by another mineral as it forms. Much of the golden material comes from Bahia State, and at the January 2017 Jewelry Industry Summit in Tucson, Brian and Kendra Cook of Nature's Geometry described work with 2,500 miners toward a collective at Remedios in Novo Horizonte, with a warehouse, cutting facilities and a visitor center. In the United States, the name Herkimer diamond properly belongs to double-terminated quartz from Herkimer County, New York; the short, faceted look it inspired is Herkimer-style. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.lore: Rutilated quartz has been called Venus' Hair Stone, after the fine gold threads suspended in the clear body. That name has traveled with the stone for a long time, and the inclusions are what people talk about first: the same needles a cutter would remove from another gem are the reason this one gets picked up. In crystal tradition, rock crystal is given the title "master healer." It is a folk name, offered here as tradition and nothing more. People have long kept clear quartz close, and the old names stayed attached to it as it passed from hand to hand.
crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.uses: Clear quartz is the workhorse spacer, the bead you set between colors to give the eye a rest, and the one makers use when they want white sparkle without diamonds. Rutilated quartz behaves like a neutral with something going on inside it. Faceted pears at 9x15mm hang well from ear wires and read from across a room. A 7mm rondelle strand runs easily as a full necklace or as breaks in a strung piece. Tubes suit drop earrings and simple pendants. We list seven strands. In the rutilated, dense bright gold needles spread evenly through the bead give the strongest flash; sparse brown ones stay quiet.
crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.care: Quartz sits at 7 on the Mohs scale, hard enough for everyday wear. Wash in warm soapy water with a soft brush, and an ultrasonic is fine. Watch the drill holes on rutilated beads, since a rutile needle that reaches the surface can chip there. Dry a strand fully before putting it away.
crystal-quartz-and-golden-rutilated-quar.tagline: Clear stone, gold needles, cold in the hand.

smoky-and-cognac-quartz.opening: Hold a strand to a window and the brown reads clear through it, tea at the light end, cola at the dark. Cognac is the warm middle, a gold-brown like a maple leaf on the day it turns. Faceted, the small planes catch and throw sparks in a color that stays quiet. Makers reach for it because it sits well beside copper and black leather, and because a good strand asks very little of a budget.
smoky-and-cognac-quartz.history: The brown comes from natural radiation given off by the surrounding rock, working on traces of aluminum caught in the quartz. The Cairngorm Mountains in Scotland gave the stone one of its old names, cairngorm. Fine crystals have long come from St. Gotthard in Switzerland. It is found in Brazil and Madagascar, and Colorado produces it as well. Because it is common and often comes clean and large, smoky quartz was never an important gemstone in earlier centuries. It found a place in jewelry only in recent times, and mostly as an affordable one. Cognac is a bead-trade name rather than a separate variety, used for the warm golden-brown end of the range, a matter of tone. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India. We choose them strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
smoky-and-cognac-quartz.lore: In crystal tradition smoky quartz is called a grounding stone, the one people are told to hold when they feel scattered or pulled in too many directions. It is said to draw the attention back down into the body and the day at hand, the way a heavy coat settles a person in wind. The dark end of the color gets much of the credit in that telling, since brown is the color people associate with soil and bark and the underside of things. Those who follow the tradition often keep a piece somewhere ordinary, in a pocket or on a desk, so it comes to hand without ceremony. These are beliefs carried along with the stone.
smoky-and-cognac-quartz.uses: Faceted hearts and pears do the most work here. We stock them at 4x6mm and 7mm. The smaller stones run through a strand as spacing between metal or wood, and a single one drops well from a chain. The larger size holds a center in a bracelet, or makes a pair of earrings with weight but not bulk. Brown carries neutral palettes and autumn lines, and it turns up often in men's bracelets. It partners with citrine for very little. A stronger strand shows even color bead to bead, clear enough to read through, with each facet giving a distinct flash rather than a dull glow. We currently list two strands.
smoky-and-cognac-quartz.care: At 7 on the Mohs scale this is an everyday stone that takes ordinary wear well. Warm water with a little mild soap and a soft brush is enough, and an ultrasonic cleaner is fine. Keep it away from strong heat, whether a dashboard in summer sun or a torch on the bench, since heat can lighten the brown.
smoky-and-cognac-quartz.tagline: A brown you can read straight through.

rainbow-moonstone.opening: On the strand it reads almost white, a row of small glassy panes with a little cloud held inside each one. Then you tilt the string toward a window and the blue arrives, bead after bead, and switches off again as you turn away. That tilt is why people reach for it. A few beads carry a flick of gold or violet along one edge. Cut with facets, the sheen breaks into short bright points instead of one soft billow.
rainbow-moonstone.history: Rainbow moonstone is white labradorite, a plagioclase feldspar of sodium, calcium and aluminum silicate. Classic moonstone is a different member of the family, orthoclase, where light scattering between alternating thin layers of orthoclase and albite makes the soft floating glow called adularescence, named because it looks like the moon behind thin cloud. Nearly all commercial moonstone of that older kind comes from the Dumbara District of Sri Lanka. Labradorite scatters light off its own thin internal layers, which is why the color runs to blue and sometimes further, and the trade has long accepted it as a gem in its own right. Some buyers now prefer it to the traditional stone. The rough behind bead strands is mostly Indian. Ours are cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
rainbow-moonstone.lore: In Hindu mythology moonstone is described as solidified moonbeams, and cultures far from one another have tied the stone to moonlight. Old legends hold that it brings good luck, and it was once believed that holding a moonstone in your mouth during a full moon would let you see what was coming. In crystal tradition, rainbow moonstone is the stone of new beginnings, carried at thresholds and turning points, and people have long believed it steadies the person wearing it. Moonstone is a June birthstone, one of the original modern birthstones set in 1912, sharing the month with pearl and alexandrite. That connection is why it turns up so often in gifts given for a birthday or a start.
rainbow-moonstone.uses: Bridal, celestial and boho makers keep coming back to it, and the shapes that move fastest here are faceted rondelles and briolettes. Rondelles at 3 to 4mm work as spacers and as a full white line in a strung necklace, bright without shouting. Pear briolettes around 9x15mm hang well for earrings, single drops or a fringe. Coins suit a statement piece where you want the sheen read as one broad plane. On a strong strand the blue lifts across most of the beads rather than showing on two or three while the rest sit chalky. We list four strands.
rainbow-moonstone.care: Wear it in earrings and necklaces rather than a bracelet that takes knocks. At 6 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale, with perfect cleavage, a hard hit can split a bead along its grain. Clean with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry it. Keep it out of ultrasonic machines and away from steam.
rainbow-moonstone.tagline: Roll it under the light and find the blue.

strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.opening: Hold a strand to a window and the two halves of the name separate. Strawberry quartz lets light through, a clear body carrying red flecks and fine needles that look suspended mid-drift. Red aventurine stops the light: brick red, opaque, with a faint glitter that shifts as you turn a bead between your fingers. On the wrist both read as warm red, one lit from inside, the other from the surface. Two materials share the one loose name.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.history: Both belong to the quartz family. Strawberry quartz is a trade name for quartz colored pink to red by inclusions large enough to see, usually small platelets or hair-like crystals of hematite that grew inside the crystal while it formed. The more inclusions there are, and the more evenly they spread, the deeper the red reads. Red aventurine is quartzite rather than a single crystal, colored by hematite with flakes of mica; light entering the stone bounces off those flakes and produces the sparkle called aventurescence. The name aventurine comes from the Italian a ventura, by chance, after a copper-flecked glass first made by accident in Italy in the early 18th century. India supplies most of the aventurine in the bead trade. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California. Cherry quartz, sold under a similar sounding name, is glass. These are stone.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.lore: Crystal tradition keeps these two in the same company and gives them the same word: love. Strawberry quartz is described as a stone of affection, gentle where other red stones are loud. Red aventurine is spoken of in terms of vitality, the liveliness people have long read into the color red. Much of this arrived with the trade names rather than from old texts, since strawberry quartz is a fairly new name in the gem world. That is still how the beads travel. Sellers set them out together in February, and people choose them for pieces about love. All of it is custom and belief, carried along with the stones.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.uses: These beads suit pink and red bracelet stacks, and they turn up every winter in Valentine's lines. Faceted teardrops at 11x15mm hang well from ear wires, where the red catches at every turn of the head. Small 5x8mm rondelles work as spacers between larger stones, breaking up a strand of jasper or clear quartz without crowding it. Hearts read plainly for what they are and need no help from the rest of the piece. Strawberry quartz next to red aventurine gives you two reds in one bracelet, one lit through, one matte with a glint. We list seven strands, sold by the sixteen inch and the eight.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.care: Everyday durable, both of them, which is why they hold up in bracelets that get worn daily. Warm water and a little soap on a soft cloth is enough, and an ultrasonic is fine. Red aventurine is slightly porous, so keep harsh household cleaners away from it and dry the strand before storing.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.tagline: Two stones share one name, and the red grew inside.
strawberry-quartz-and-red-aventurine.judge: Draft B pulls in more concrete fact-pack details (strand count, pricing units, sensory specifics) and reads with a steadier, more grounded voice while keeping lore framed as tradition. (a 36, b 39)
