peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.opening: Hold a strand up and tilt it. The peach beads warm from apricot to cream, the gray ones shift from smoke to silver, and a soft light seems to travel just under each polished face rather than sit on top of it. Chocolate and golden shine hold their color in the body, with the sheen crossing over the top of it. People reach for these because the glow moves when the wearer moves. Next to plain silver, the gray looks like weather.
peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.history: All four colors are orthoclase, the same potassium feldspar as the pale moonstone most people picture, with the formula (K,Na)AlSi3O8. As the mineral forms, orthoclase and albite separate into alternating layers thin enough that light falling between them scatters instead of passing through. GIA calls the result adularescence, light that appears to billow across a gem. Other feldspars, labradorite and sanidine among them, can show the same effect. Trace iron supplies the body color, which is what sets peach, gray, chocolate and golden shine apart from the colorless material. Nearly all of this rough comes out of India, and the colored cabochons that made the range familiar to buyers were cut from Indian stone. Its glow has held attention for centuries. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen one strand at a time in Cupertino, California.
peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.lore: In Hindu mythology, moonstone is said to be made of solidified moonbeams, and many other cultures have tied the stone to moonlight for the same plain reason: the sheen looks like a full moon behind thin high cloud. Old legends hold that it brings good luck to the person carrying it. One belief said you could see what was coming if you held a moonstone in your mouth during a full moon. In crystal tradition it is kept as the stone of the moon and of calm, something to wear when you want a quieter mood. Moonstone is a birthstone for June, alongside pearl and alexandrite.
peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.uses: Designers working in neutrals and earth tones tend to start with peach, which suits bridal work, while the gray goes to minimalist silver pieces. Faceted pears and marquise are the shapes makers ask for most in earrings, and we keep them in 11x15mm and 10x14mm. Heishi is the bracelet shape. We list 57 strands across faceted, smooth and organic cuts, pears and marquise by the 8 inch strand, heishi by the 16. A better bead has clean body color and a sheen that travels as you turn it; flat beads with no movement sit at the bottom of the range.
peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.care: Keep these to earrings and pendants. Two cleavage directions mean the beads chip under a knock, so we steer people away from rings. At 6 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale, they scratch more easily than quartz. Clean with warm soapy water and a soft cloth. No ultrasonic machine, no steam, no sudden heat.
peach-gray-chocolate-and-golden-shine-mo.tagline: Color in the body, moonlight moving under the surface.

sunstone.opening: On the strand, sunstone shows warm apricot and rust with islands of metallic sparkle. Tilt it and the glitter comes in patches, not all at once. Those bright points come from tiny flat platelets of hematite or copper that grew inside the feldspar. It reads like late light across a field. Makers reach for it when a piece needs warmth with texture, or a quiet flash that appears and disappears as the wearer moves.
sunstone.history: Sunstone is a feldspar. Both orthoclase and the plagioclase species have sunstone varieties, including oligoclase. Bead-grade material comes from Tamil Nadu, India, and Tanzania. Deposits are also known at Tvedestrand, Norway; near Lake Baikal, Russia; and in the United States at Middletown, Pennsylvania, and Statesville, North Carolina. Oregon sunstone, a transparent feldspar with glittery copper inclusions, has gained attention as a product of the United States. The aventurescent effect arises from minute plate-like inclusions, commonly hematite or copper, aligned in the crystal; light reflects from them at a common angle to produce a flash. The stone is often cut en cabochon. In beads, the effect shows as moving patches along a strand. A glass imitation called goldstone sparkles uniformly from every angle and can show bubbles, sometimes in blue or green; natural sunstone never does.
sunstone.lore: In crystal tradition, sunstone has been linked with the warmth and power of the sun. People have long believed it brings energy, vitality, joy, and a steady sense of personal power. The glittering inclusions suggested stored sunlight to many, so it was kept for joy and personal power. Medieval sources in Iceland describe a mineral called a sunstone used to locate the sun in overcast skies, and church inventories in the 14th and 15th centuries in Iceland and Germany also mention sunstones. Today, it is kept, in crystal circles, for joy and personal power, as tradition holds.
sunstone.uses: We stock square heishi, flat nuggets, and faceted rondelles. The square heishi make easy men's bracelets; the flat nuggets read bold on cord or leather. Faceted 5 mm rondelles show the patchy flash as they turn, and 9 x 15 mm flat nuggets make it easy to see that effect along the strand. It settles into warm autumn and southwestern palettes, and pairs cleanly with labradorite. We have our strands cut in Jaipur, India, then choose them strand by strand in Cupertino, California. A stronger flash shows as dense coppery patches that light up as the bead turns.
sunstone.care: With two cleavage directions and a Mohs hardness near 6 to 6.5, sunstone is best in earrings and necklaces. Avoid hard knocks that can chip edges. Clean with warm soapy water and a soft cloth. Skip ultrasonic and steam. Store strands apart from harder stones to keep surfaces from scuffing.

amazonite.opening: Hold a strand of amazonite up to the window and the color sits still. Blue-green, opaque, with no glow coming through from behind. The Russian beads carry white albite stripes, some in a grid, some in ribbons. Because light does not pass through the stone, what you end up looking at is the cutting: flat faces, clean edges, a low steady sheen along the polish. People reach for it when a design wants turquoise blue and a stone that stands on its own name.
amazonite.history: Amazonite is microcline, a potassium feldspar, KAlSi3O8, its color thought to come from trace lead and water in the structure. The name came from the Amazon River, where green stones were once believed to have been obtained, though no deposit has been found there and it remains uncertain whether those stones were amazonite at all. People have worn it for more than three thousand years, as archaeological finds in Middle and New Kingdom Egypt and in Mesopotamia show, and it is not named by any ancient or medieval writer. For a long stretch it was confused with jade, which the color explains. The stone comes today from the Ilmen Mountains in Russia, and from Peru and Brazil. Russian material shows the white striping and goes by the name Russian banded; plain blue is not Russian. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
amazonite.lore: In crystal tradition amazonite is held to be a stone of hope, and people have long believed that is what it brings the wearer. The belief is usually left at that one word, with no list attached to it. It is handed down by word of mouth, repeated from one pair of hands to the next, and offered as belief rather than as a finding. Nothing in it is measured or proved. Makers who care about such things tend to say the word plainly when they hand a finished piece over, and then leave the rest of it to the person who wears it.
amazonite.uses: Marquise and pear suit earrings, since the long faces show the polish, and we stock both at 10x13mm and 10x15mm. Rectangles go to designers working geometric and plain. The color belongs to summer and coastal palettes, and it gives you turquoise blue in a necklace. We carry amazonite faceted and smooth, in marquise, pear and rectangle among other shapes, including the Russian banded, with 32 strands listed at a time and sold by the 8 inch and the 16 inch. On the Russian line, saturated teal with crisp white banding is the strongest look; Peruvian material runs paler turquoise blue.
amazonite.care: Amazonite is 6 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale with two cleavage directions, so it chips on a hard knock rather than wearing down slowly. Keep it to earrings, necklaces and light bracelets. Wash with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry it. No ultrasonic, no steam.
amazonite.tagline: A hope stone the color of shallow water.

rhodolite-garnet.opening: Hold a strand of rhodolite up to a window and the color reads raspberry, with a cool purple edge running through the red. Not brick. Not the brown of the garnets most people picture. The faceted rondelles are small and tightly cut, and light comes back off them in short flashes rather than a broad glow, so a whole strand seems to flicker as it turns. Most beads are clean enough to look straight through. Roll one between thumb and finger and the facets catch on the skin.
rhodolite-garnet.history: Rhodolite is a pyrope-almandine garnet, a magnesium-iron aluminum silicate that sits between the two species and always carries small amounts of others besides. The name comes from the Greek rhodon, rose-like. Hidden and Pratt gave it in 1898 to a rose-red garnet found in detrital sands at Masons Branch Brook in Cowee Valley, Macon County, North Carolina. It is a trade name, not an official mineral species, kept in use because the purplish red hue is worth naming. Red garnets go back much further in jewelry: necklaces buried with Egypt's pharaohs, carved signet rings in Rome that stamped the wax on important documents, and wide use in Pliny's time, from 23 to 79 AD. The bead material comes from elsewhere now. Tanzania, Mozambique, Sri Lanka, Odisha in India, Madagascar. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, then chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
rhodolite-garnet.lore: Garnet is the birthstone for January, and rhodolite is often the choice for people who want that custom without a dark red stone. Tradition makes garnet a stone given between friends. People have long believed it keeps a traveler safe on the road. Older writing called red garnets carbuncle, a name used loosely for almost any red stone, and one story holds that carbuncle was among the four precious stones given to King Solomon by God. None of this is asked of a bead on the bench. It comes along anyway, and plenty of makers like knowing it is there.
rhodolite-garnet.uses: Faceted 3mm rondelles are the workhorse. They sit tight between knots, hold their color at that small scale, and carry a full necklace or a wrapped bracelet without going heavy. Pear briolettes move just as fast, and the 5x8mm we stock is the size makers keep coming back to for earring drops. The pink-red sits well against gold fill. It also holds its own against oxidized silver. A stronger strand shows even raspberry with a purple flash in daylight, no brown creeping in, and beads that are eye-clean and unchipped at the hole. Smooth ovals are here too, for anyone who wants the color without the sparkle.
rhodolite-garnet.care: Rhodolite runs 7 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale with no cleavage. That is hard enough for daily wear, and hard enough that the stone will outlast the wire it is strung on. Wash it in warm soapy water with a soft brush. Dry it before you put it away.
rhodolite-garnet.tagline: The purple-red garnet, cut small and worn often.
rhodolite-garnet.judge: Draft B grounds its history and care sections in more precise sourced details (Masons Branch Brook, no cleavage, species blending) and keeps a plainer, less promotional voice than Draft A. (a 32, b 39)

red-mozambique-garnet.opening: On a strand it reads as one steady color: red with a faint orange warmth, the kind that stays red under a lamp instead of going brown. Faceted rondelles throw small bright points along the whole length. Smooth ovals sit quieter and deeper, and the larger ones look almost black until you lift them toward a window and the center opens up. People reach for this stone because the red is plain and honest, never tipping toward purple.
red-mozambique-garnet.history: The material sold as Mozambique garnet comes from that country's deposits, and it is almandine-pyrope, an iron-magnesium aluminum silicate that sits between the two garnet species. Red garnet from India and Sri Lanka gets mixed into parcels along the way, which is one reason a single bag can hold slightly different reds. Garnet itself is among the oldest gems in use. The Ancient Egyptians set almandine in jewelry as early as 3,500 BCE, and red garnet necklaces were buried with mummified pharaohs as prized possessions for the afterlife. In Rome, signet rings with carved garnets stamped the wax that closed important documents, and by Pliny's time, 23 to 79 AD, red garnets were among the most widely worn stones. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
red-mozambique-garnet.lore: In older writing, red garnets were often called carbuncle, a name applied to almost any red stone, and tradition holds that carbuncle was one of the four precious stones given to King Solomon by God. Cultures across the world have kept garnet close for its color and its durability, and the associations that grew up around it are love, friendship, light, and vitality. In crystal tradition it is worn as a stone of loyalty between friends, and people have long believed the red carries courage along with it. Garnet is the traditional birthstone for January and the gem given for a second anniversary.
red-mozambique-garnet.uses: Faceted rondelles move fastest, and 3mm is the size makers keep coming back to: a 16 inch strand runs about 35 carats, enough for a fine line of red between silver spacers or as a seed row beside pearls. At 8mm the same shape becomes a bracelet bead, heavy enough to hold its own on a wrist and a steady seller for holiday pieces. Smooth ovals suit longer necklaces where you want mass and depth rather than sparkle, and a 16 inch strand of them runs 150 to 200 carats. Small pears work as drops on earring wires or as an end accent. We carry all three shapes, tagged.
red-mozambique-garnet.care: Garnet takes daily wear well. At 7 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale it resists scratching, and it has no cleavage, so a knock is unlikely to split a bead. Wash with mild soap, warm water, and a soft brush, then dry the strand flat before you store or string it.
red-mozambique-garnet.tagline: The classic garnet red, cut in Jaipur, chosen here.
red-mozambique-garnet.judge: Draft B delivers more concrete, jewelry-specific detail and tighter lore framing, while both drafts add a few unsupported flourishes but B's are more grounded in the sourced facts. (a 35, b 38)

hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.opening: Hold a shaded strand to a window and the beads sort themselves out: cinnamon at one end, honey through the middle, then a few that go clean mandarin. Under a 10x loupe the hessonite gives itself away. The inside looks stirred, a swirled, oily texture that cutters call treacle. Citrine by comparison sits glassy and empty, and lighter in the hand. People reach for these strands in autumn, when they want orange that stands up to being worn every day.
hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.history: Hessonite belongs to the grossular species, a calcium aluminum silicate, and arrives in cinnamon and honey tones from Sri Lanka, India and Tanzania. Spessartite is a different chemistry, manganese aluminum silicate, and takes its name from Spessart in Bavaria, Germany, where it was first described. The brighter mandarin material comes from Nigeria, Namibia and Mozambique. Garnet has been worn a long time. Red garnet necklaces were placed on the necks of Egypt's pharaohs and buried with them for the afterlife, and in Rome carved garnets set into signet rings stamped the wax that secured documents. By Pliny's day, 23 to 79 AD, red garnets were among the most widely traded gems. Grossular took much longer to find an audience, and for years hessonite was the only part of the species used much in jewelry. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.lore: Garnet is the birthstone for January and the gem given for a second anniversary. In older writing the word carbuncle covered red garnets and nearly any red stone, and one tradition holds that carbuncle was among the four precious stones given to King Solomon. Across many cultures people have long associated garnet with love, friendship, light and vitality, and have worn it as a stone of warmth and steadiness. In India, hessonite is known as gomed and is worn by tradition for the planet Rahu, which is why buyers who follow Vedic astrology often ask for it by that name. These are beliefs carried down through generations rather than statements about the stone itself.
hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.uses: Faceted rondelles at 3 to 4mm do the most work here: spacers between larger stones, a whole strand knotted for a plain necklace, short runs in earrings. Shaded heishi is the other steady seller, since the drift from cinnamon to mandarin along the strand does the design work for you. Pear briolettes at 7x13mm suit a single drop or a close-set fringe. Autumn palettes take most of what we sell, and a shaded parcel lets one necklace run through several tones without anything needing to match. We list three strands at a time.
hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.care: These take daily wear. Garnet sits at 6.5 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale, hard enough for a necklace worn most days. Wash with mild soap and water, then dry the beads before they go back on the hook. Store them apart from harder stones so the facet edges stay crisp.
hessonite-and-spessartite-garnet.tagline: Fire opal color at garnet hardness.

peridot.opening: Hold a strand of peridot up to a window and the whole thing reads one color: green with a squeeze of yellow in it, no brown anywhere. Peridot is one of the few stones that comes in a single hue, so the beads along a strand match each other without much sorting. Look closely and you may find flat disc inclusions like small lily pads, or a scatter of black specks. Those belong there. At 3mm the color stays light and lit.
peridot.history: Peridot is gem olivine, the magnesium-rich forsterite end of the family, and iron is what turns it green. Most of it formed deep inside the earth and rode to the surface in volcanoes; some arrived in meteorites. On Oahu, small pieces wash ashore near volcanic ground. The ancient Egyptians mined it on Zabargad, an island in the Red Sea, and that deposit supplied many of the large fine stones now in museums; a 146.10-carat peridot sits in the Natural History Museum in London. The English name is unsettled in origin, traced by some to Anglo-Norman pedoretés and by others to the Arabic faridat, meaning gemstone, with the earliest English use possibly in 1705. Bead material today comes mostly from Hebei in China and Kohistan in Pakistan, with San Carlos in Arizona supplying small sizes. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
peridot.lore: The Egyptians called peridot the gem of the sun. Some held that it kept its owner safe from the terrors of the night, and that the protection was stronger when the stone was set in gold. Others strung the gems on donkey hair and tied them around the left arm to turn away evil spirits. Legends have long tied peridot to sunlight, and with it energy and happiness for the wearer. In Hawaiian stories the green grains near the lava rock were tears of Pele, goddess of the elements, said to fall from the sky with the rain. Crystal tradition still holds that peridot wards off nightmares. It is one of the August birthstones and the gem for a fifteenth anniversary.
peridot.uses: Faceted 3mm rondelles do most of the work here. Strung plain they make a light green line at the throat, and they sit well between freshwater pearls for a spring palette or against gold for an olive-and-gold one. Pear briolettes in 4x6mm hang clean as earrings, one to a wire, and they take a bail without much fuss. Ovals read longer than the rondelles and break up a plain strand. We carry faceted 3mm rondelles and ovals, plus pear briolettes on eight-inch strands, and we look over the drill holes for chipping before a strand goes on the tag.
peridot.care: Peridot sits at 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale and it is brittle, so it takes knocks poorly. Necklaces and earrings are easy; wear a bracelet with some care and keep it off hard surfaces. Clean with mild soap and water and a soft cloth. No ultrasonic, no steam, no acids.
peridot.tagline: One color only, from volcano rock to finished strand.

apatite.opening: Apatite comes onto the strand in a blue-green so saturated it looks lit from inside, closer to pool water at night than to sky. Hold a strand up. The beads read translucent, not milky, with fine needle inclusions crossing the light. No two are quite alike. One bead leans teal, its neighbor leans blue. It has heft, noticeably more than glass or quartz of the same size. Makers reach for it when they want that electric color without a tourmaline budget.
apatite.history: Apatite is not one mineral but a group of calcium phosphates, built with fluorine, chlorine or hydroxyl in the same crystal frame. It is common. Most of what comes out of the ground goes into phosphate for fertilizer and acids rather than into rings, and it also makes up much of the teeth and bones of vertebrate animals. The German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner named it in 1786, borrowing the Greek word for deceiving, because good crystals are so easily mistaken for other stones. In 1860 the German mineralogist Karl Friedrich August Rammelsberg reclassified the material Werner had described as fluorapatite. Clear blue-green crystals have long been faceted for collectors. At Mohs 5, though, the stone stayed a specialist's gem. The neon blue to teal bead material we buy comes from Madagascar. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, then chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
apatite.lore: In crystal tradition apatite is kept as a stone for motivation. People are said to reach for it when a project has gone quiet and needs picking up again. Those who follow that tradition speak of it as encouragement rather than luck or protection, something to hold on a morning when you are deciding what to make next. The idea travels with the stone. Often someone hands over a strand and mentions it in the same breath, as though the color and the belief arrived together and cannot easily be separated now. None of this is offered as fact. It is folklore, held a long time and passed along as such.
apatite.uses: Faceted rondelles do the most work here. The small facets catch light and push the color forward on a plain wire or a short chain. Our 4x6mm faceted teardrops suit earrings, one to a hook, or a single drop at the center of a necklace. Smooth 8mm rondelles give a weightier strand with less sparkle and more body, good against oxidized silver or brass. Designers come to apatite for Paraiba-tourmaline color at bead prices, and they accept that every strand varies a little; that variation is how you know it is stone. In a stronger strand the blue-green runs deep and even, and light passes through it.
apatite.care: Keep apatite in earrings and necklaces rather than bracelets. It is brittle, and at 5 on the Mohs scale a quartz point scratches it easily. Wipe with a damp cloth and nothing more. No ultrasonic cleaner, no heat, no acids. Slight chipping at the drill holes is normal in real stone.
apatite.tagline: Neon blue-green from Madagascar, cut small and worn gently.
apatite.judge: Draft B sticks closer to the sourced facts (no added care advice or speculative claims) while still delivering concrete, sensory detail and a clean tradition-framed lore section. (a 38, b 42)

iolite.opening: Iolite on a strand looks like denim washed a few times, blue with gray in it. Turn the strand and the color shifts: one face inky violet-blue, the next pale and watery, the third a hint of straw. That flicker belongs to the stone, not to the light. Glass can be blue, but glass cannot do that. Makers reach for iolite when they want a sapphire look at a working price, on a bead that holds its color across a whole necklace.
iolite.history: Mineralogists call it cordierite, a magnesium-iron aluminum silicate. The mineral was described in 1813 from specimens at Níjar, in Almería, Spain, and named for the French geologist Louis Cordier, who lived from 1777 to 1861. The gem trade uses a different name, iolite, from the Greek word for violet. Older names stuck to it as well. Dichroite means two-colored rock, and water sapphire came from the same habit of changing color as you turn it, blue from one direction and nearly clear from another. Most of the bead material we see comes from India, with some out of Tanzania and Sri Lanka. Because the rough is usually transparent and fairly clean, it is most often faceted, though it is also cut as cabochons and carvings, and it turns up often as beads. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen one at a time in Cupertino, California.
iolite.lore: Legend gives iolite a job at sea. Viking navigators are said to have used thin slices of it as a filter, cutting glare and locating the sun through overcast sky so they could fix their own position. Whether that ever happened is unsettled, and the tale is passed along as tradition rather than record, but the name Viking compass stone has stayed with it. The nickname holds the idea in it: light read through a blue stone, direction found on a day with no sun in view. Iolite has long been fashioned for adornment, and in the language of anniversaries it belongs to the twenty-first year.
iolite.uses: Iolite sits in denim and slate palettes and does the work of a sapphire look in an everyday necklace. Faceted heishi at 4mm moves fastest here; the flat discs pack tight and keep the blue coming and going down the whole line. Smooth ovals at 8x10mm suit a plain strung necklace or a knotted piece with silver in it. When you pick a strand, hold it at arm's length. The drilling decides which face shows, and on the better strands nearly every bead reads blue from the front. We have eight strands in the shop, in sixteen inch lengths and half strands of eight inches.
iolite.care: Iolite runs 7 to 7.5 on the Mohs scale, hard enough for daily wear. It has one direction of cleavage, so a sharp knock against a counter edge matters more than a scratch. Wash with mild soap and warm water. Store it where it will not press against harder stones.
iolite.tagline: Turn it and the blue comes and goes.

kyanite.opening: A strand of blue kyanite reads in bands, darker in one spot and paler in the next. Faceted rondelles throw a cold, hard blue that comes close to sapphire. The box beads and smooth ovals are sliced parallel to the blade, so each one shows a wide flat face with a glassy polish. Blades hold their color unevenly, and on a strand that shows as a run of light and dark. Makers reach for it when they want that blue at a working price.
kyanite.history: Kyanite is an aluminum silicate that grows as flat blades in metamorphic rock, formed when clay minerals are altered under high pressure. It turns up in schists and gneisses, less often in quartzite or eclogite, and points to metamorphism deep in the crust. The name comes from the Greek kyanos, meaning blue. Older books call it disthene, two strengths, since the blade runs about 4.5 to 5 along its length and 6.5 to 7 across it. That, with perfect cleavage in one direction, kept it a cutter's puzzle and a collector's stone, with cut gems reaching ten to fifteen carats. Gem material long came from Brazil, Cambodia and Burma, usually gray toned and seldom clear. Finds in Nepal brought blue that rivals fine sapphire. Blue is now mainly Nepalese and Indian; Brazil and East Africa give teal. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
kyanite.lore: In crystal tradition, one claim about kyanite outruns the rest: that it never needs cleansing. People who keep stones say it does not hold what passes through it, so it is never put through the clearing that other stones traditionally get. That is tradition rather than fact, but it is the first thing many collectors will tell you about the blue blades, and it is why kyanite often shares a pouch with stones that are given a regular clearing. The old name, disthene, points at the other thing people remark on: two strengths in one crystal, soft along its length and hard across it. Blue and hard to cut, it has long been a stone collectors keep for themselves.
kyanite.uses: Faceted rondelles and pears move fastest, mostly with designers after sapphire blue at a working price. A 4mm rondelle strand runs about 55 carats per 16 inches and gives a fine, even line of blue. The 9 to 10mm pears come on 8 inch strands. Box beads suit long necklaces where the flat faces can lie against the skin, and come on strands of about 200 carats. We carry blue, teal and multi. On a stronger strand the color is even from end to end and the flat face takes a bright polish, so the blue looks lit rather than flat.
kyanite.care: Best in necklaces and earrings. Bracelets wear the soft direction of the blade quickly, and a knock along the length can split a bead, so beads drilled across the blade hold up better. Watch the edges for white flaky spots, which are early cleavage. Wash in mild soap and water.
kyanite.tagline: Blades of Nepal blue, soft one way and hard the other.

lapis-lazuli.opening: On the strand, lapis reads as a run of deep navy with small gold sparks scattered through it. The gold is pyrite, and it is the surest sign you are holding lapis and not something else. Some beads carry a thin gray-white cloud of calcite; others are almost solid blue. Faceted rondelles catch light in short flashes along the edges, while smooth rounds go quiet and matte-dark, like ink. People reach for it because the blue holds its own next to gold wire.
lapis-lazuli.history: Lapis is a rock rather than a single mineral, an aggregate of lazurite with calcite and pyrite, plus small amounts of diopside, amphibole, feldspar, or mica. Lazurite gives the royal blue. It was mined in the mountains of Badakhshan, in what is now Afghanistan, as early as the 7th millennium BC, and historians place the link between people and this stone at more than 6,500 years. It was valued in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Greece, and Rome, prized alongside sapphire and turquoise, and cut for inlay and intarsia as well as ground for pigment and cosmetics. By 700 BC the region was known as Bactria; Marco Polo described its mines in 1271, and the same workings still produce. Chile supplies most of the paler, calcite-rich denim grade. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
lapis-lazuli.lore: Lapis legends are among the oldest recorded. In older gem tradition the stone stands for truth, and that is the association people who work with it repeat most often. Some accounts link lapis to mother goddess figures of the ancient world. Pliny the Elder, writing in Rome, called it a fragment of the starry firmament, in admiration of the deep blue with its twinkling bits of gold. Scholars believe many early references to sapphire may in fact describe lapis, which says something about how the blue was ranked. Jewelry made from it has been found in prehistoric tombs in Asia, Africa, and Europe. Older birthstone lists name it for December.
lapis-lazuli.uses: Faceted 5mm rondelles are the workhorse. They build a full navy line without weight, and they space well with small gold or brass beads. Smooth 8mm rounds suit men's bracelets and single-strand necklaces where you want the blue solid and unbroken. Daggers make a fringe for a collar or a pair of long earrings. Lapis sits easily in navy-and-gold palettes, and paler denim-grade material softens a design when full royal blue feels too heavy. Stronger strands show deep royal blue with gold flecks and almost no visible white; middle grades carry more pyrite and gray calcite spotting.
lapis-lazuli.care: At 5 to 6 on the Mohs scale, lapis marks more easily than quartz. Pendants and earrings take daily wear; bracelets need more care, since cuffs and desks scuff beads. Clean with mild soap and a soft brush, then dry well. Keep it away from ultrasonic cleaners and solvents.
lapis-lazuli.tagline: Deep blue with gold pyrite, cut in Jaipur.

larimar.opening: Hold a strand of larimar up to a window. The blue shifts bead to bead: pale sky in one, something closer to deep water in the next, white cloud moving through both. Some lean green. Some go almost turquoise. The pattern comes from fibers that grew in radiating sprays, so the white spreads in feathered lines rather than flat patches. Makers reach for it because the color reads as water from across a room, and because the cloud gives a small bead something to look at.
larimar.history: Larimar is the trade name for blue pectolite, a sodium calcium silicate hydroxide colored by copper. Pectolite itself is not rare and turns up worldwide. But its fibrous masses are usually too soft and fragile to cut. Where the fibers grow intertwined, the material becomes jade-like in toughness, and that is the stone worth cutting. The blue kind comes from one limited deposit at Los Chupaderos near Barahona in the Dominican Republic, virtually the only gem material to come out of the Caribbean. It was first described from the Filipinas Larimar Mine at Los Checheses, in the Sierra de Baoruco, and takes its name from that locality. Dominican Ministry of Mining records note a permission request from Father Miguel Domingo Fuertes Loren of the Barahona Parish. Compact material makes good cabochons. It has stood in for turquoise. One hill, one country. When it is worked out, that is the end of it.
larimar.lore: Tradition calls larimar the Atlantis stone, on the idea that a blue stone from one Caribbean hill answers to a drowned island. That is folklore rather than history. Most people who repeat it know as much. The name has stuck all the same, and it colors how the stone is worn and given. In crystal tradition larimar is spoken of as a stone for calm, and people have long chosen it on that belief, keeping a piece close for quiet company rather than for anything they can point to. Others come to it for the color alone. Shallow water is restful to look at, and this is the color of shallow water. Collectors want it for a plainer reason: one deposit, and nowhere else.
larimar.uses: Smooth nuggets sell best. They suit larimar's habit of varying bead to bead, and a strand at 10 to 15mm makes a necklace that needs nothing added. Faceted pear briolettes go straight to earrings, where the cloud pattern reads clearly against the ear. Rondelles fill in between metal spacers when you want the blue in a smaller dose. Designers working a beach theme keep coming back to it, as do collectors of single-source stones. The strongest strands run sky blue to deep volcanic blue, with white cloud and no gray or green cast. Ours are cut in Jaipur and chosen one at a time here in Cupertino.
larimar.care: Keep larimar to necklaces and earrings, and to bracelets you can be careful with. At 4.5 to 5 on the Mohs scale, a copper coin will not scratch it but a steel pin will. The blue can fade after years in sunlight, so store the piece in the dark. No ultrasonic cleaner. No heat.
larimar.tagline: One hill in the Dominican Republic, and blue like shallow water

turquoise.opening: On a strand, turquoise looks like pieces of sky held together. Arizona type blue sits clean and bright; Golden Hills shows lavender blue with brown matrix; green stones carry fine webbing. Heishi lines wear light and even. Four millimeter rondelles stack close and smooth. Nuggets keep the hand on the stone. They feel irregular and tactile. People reach for it first for the color, then for how it settles into silver or leather and makes steady daily pieces.
turquoise.history: Turquoise forms where copper-rich water meets aluminum and phosphorus in arid ground, creating a porous, opaque gem. Bead material today comes from Arizona, China's Hubei, Iran, and, from 2013, Kazakhstan's Altyn-Tyube deposit known as Golden Hills. Arizona's Kingman mine still operates; Sleeping Beauty closed in 2012. Turquoise was mined in Egypt's Sinai before the 4th millennium BC. Rulers of ancient Egypt wore it, and Chinese artisans carved it more than 3,000 years ago. Pieces appear in ancient Egyptian tombs and in Ancestral Puebloan inlay from Chaco Canyon National Historical Park. It is the national gem of Tibet. Europe learned the name in the thirteenth century from the French pierre tourques, "Turkish stone," because material reached Europe through Turkish sources. In trade, mine names are traditional.
turquoise.lore: In crystal tradition, turquoise is a traveler's protector and a bringer of good luck. It is the traditional birthstone for December and the gem of the 11th anniversary. Many people prize the clear sky blue as a lucky color. From Afghanistan to the Zuni Pueblo, it has long been regarded as a good luck stone. Lore often speaks of warning of danger by changing or breaking. It is also said to offer protection from evil and to favor safe passage. These are enduring beliefs about what the stone may invite.
turquoise.uses: Makers reach for turquoise for clean lines and everyday wear. Heishi builds long, supple necklaces. Rondelles in 4 mm make easy spacers and soft, even strands; larger 10 to 18 mm nuggets bring the matrix forward for statement pieces. We carry Arizona type sky blue as smooth rondelles and heishi, and we keep nuggets on hand. Golden Hills lavender blue with brown matrix comes in rondelles and in nuggets. We also stock green matrix strands. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen one by one in Cupertino. Southwest and boho designers use it across the board.
turquoise.care: Mohs 5 to 6 and porous. Wipe with a damp cloth only. Keep it away from oils and perfume during wear. No ultrasonic cleaning. It is best suited to necklaces and to earrings rather than bracelets.
turquoise.tagline: Blue born of copper, worn for the road.

fluorite.opening: Hold a strand of banded fluorite up to a window and the beads read like slices of a layered cake: green giving way to violet, violet to water clear, sometimes a seam of colorless stone between. No two beads repeat, because each one is cut through a different part of the color banding. The surface takes a glassy polish that looks wet. People reach for it because it is cheerful without being loud, and because the colors are the stone's own.
fluorite.history: Fluorite is calcium fluoride, deposited in veins by hydrothermal processes and found in the fractures and cavities of some limestones and dolomites. It is common in many parts of the world, and miners call it fluorspar. The name comes from the Latin fluere, to flow, for its use as a flux in iron smelting; it was first printed under that sense in 1530, in Georgius Agricola's Bermannus. In 1852 George Gabriel Stokes named fluorescence after the mineral, some specimens of which glow under ultraviolet light. As a decorative stone it has a long English chapter: for over 1,500 years artisans worked Blue John, the Derbyshire variety banded in white, blue, violet and reddish brown, into vases and bowls. Those deposits are nearly exhausted, and a similar banded material has since been found in China, which is where almost all rainbow bead fluorite now comes from. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen in Cupertino, California.
fluorite.lore: Crystal tradition calls fluorite the genius stone. People who keep a piece on a desk, or wear it while studying, have long believed it sharpens focus and sorts a crowded mind into order. That is belief rather than fact, but it is a persistent one, and it shapes how the stone is sold and given. It reaches crystal shops as often as jewelry benches. The banding invites its own reading, since a single bead can carry several colors at once, and people tend to speak of the stone in terms of attention and clear thinking. Whatever a wearer makes of that, the colors are reason enough to keep a strand nearby.
fluorite.uses: This is a good first colored strand. Smooth rondelles in the 6 to 8mm range are the workhorse, easy to knot or string on beading wire for a simple necklace where the color changes do the work. Faceted tubes catch more light, and crisp facet junctions are worth looking for, since a rushed polish rounds them off. Heishi lies flat and reads almost like a painted line at the throat. We carry all three in banded multicolor. The best strands show saturated bands with sharp changes between them and enough transparency to see into the bead; gray or mostly colorless beads look flat next to them. Keep it to earrings and necklaces.
fluorite.care: Fluorite is Mohs 4 with perfect cleavage in four directions. House dust will scratch it, so will a key or a steel pin, and a knock against a table edge can split a bead. Wash in cool soapy water only. No ultrasonic, no heat, no acids. Treat it like glass and it will last.
fluorite.tagline: Every bead is a different slice through the color bands.
fluorite.judge: Draft B ties more of its detail directly to the fact pack (entry-tier framing, judging criteria, both talking points) and keeps a plainer, more grounded voice, while both drafts equally over-elaborate the lore beyond the sourced 'genius stone' note. (a 35, b 38)

seraphinite.opening: Dark green, close to black in low light, with silver feathers laid across the surface. Tilt a strand of 4mm rondelles under a lamp and the feathers move: short downy tufts in one spot, long flight feathers in another. The green reads deep, not gray. Beads this small stack into a line that looks like plumage seen edge on. It is among the softest beads sold. Makers reach for it because nothing else on the tray has that pattern.
seraphinite.history: Seraphinite is a trade name rather than a mineral name. The mineral is clinochlore, a member of the chlorite group, a magnesium iron aluminum silicate. What makes it a gem material is structure: fibers that radiate in plumes, with mica giving the silvery, feathery sheen over the dark green body. The material comes from the Korshunovskoye iron mine in Irkutsk Oblast, Eastern Siberia. One mine, nowhere else. The name points to the seraphim, described in tradition as the highest rank of angels, because on good pieces the growth reads as short down leading into longer flight feathers. Sellers have built phrases on that resemblance, including silver plume seraphinite. The stone is worked for carving and as a decorative material, and used as a minor gem. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
seraphinite.lore: Crystal tradition calls this an angel stone, and the name is the reason. The seraphim originate in ancient Judaism and go on to play a part in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, where tradition places them in the highest rank of celestial beings. Whoever first polished the material saw down and flight feathers in the fibers and named it for them, and crystal sellers and collectors have carried that association along ever since. It is said to be a stone of angelic company, and people keep it near for that reason more than any other. All of this is belief and folklore, attached to the stone by its name and its pattern rather than proven by it.
seraphinite.uses: Small is the whole story here. We carry smooth 4mm rondelles and 4mm heishi, and those two shapes cover almost everything makers do with the stone, because larger beads chip and wear badly. Earrings are the natural home: a short drop, a cluster, a few beads above a hoop where they catch lamplight when the head turns. Short necklaces worn now and then work too. Keep the findings plain and let the feathers carry the piece. A stronger strand shows silver that travels as you tilt it, instead of sitting in fixed pale patches on gray-green.
seraphinite.care: A fingernail can mark it, so treat it as an occasional-wear stone: earrings and short necklaces, never bracelets, where cuffs and desk edges do their damage. Wipe with a dry or barely damp cloth. No soaking, no cleaners. Chlorite is layered and can peel, so handle the beads gently at the drill holes.
seraphinite.tagline: Silver feathers on deep green, from one Siberian mine.
seraphinite.judge: Draft B weaves in more specific, source-grounded details (mine exclusivity, seraphim rank, feather description) while keeping lore clearly framed as tradition, giving it an edge in specificity and lore handling. (a 39, b 42)

chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.opening: On the strand, two blues take turns. Chrysocolla runs robin's-egg to sky, blue-green, waxy where the polish sits and glassy where the quartz took over. Shattuckite comes in deeper. Near-royal, in fibrous patches that read almost navy in low light, often edged with black or green. People reach for it because it looks like turquoise and wears harder: copper color locked into quartz. Hold a strand up. The pale beads glow while the dark ones hold their weight.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.history: Chrysocolla forms where water carrying dissolved silica works on copper ore near the surface, so it turns up in the upper parts of copper veins in dry country. Alone it is soft. Mixed with silica as a gel and hardened into chalcedony or quartz, it reaches up to 7 on the Mohs scale, and that harder form is the one cut into beads. Ours traces back to Peru, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Arizona. Shattuckite was first found in 1915 in the copper mines of Bisbee, Arizona, at the Shattuck mine, which gave the mineral its name. Most of what reaches the market now comes from the Kaokoveld in Namibia. The name chrysocolla is older. Theophrastus and other ancient writers applied it to materials used in soldering gold, from the Greek words for gold and glue. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and picked out one at a time in Cupertino, California.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.lore: In crystal tradition these copper silicates are called stones of communication. People have long believed that keeping one close makes words easier to find, and that it favors plain speech over the polished kind. The belief travels with the beads. A strand gets strung for someone who has something to explain, or worn by a person who wants to be understood the first time and not the third. None of that is a claim about the body. It is what has been said about the stone for a long while, repeated among people who work with color and rock, and handed along with the strand itself.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.uses: Makers reach for these beads most often in Southwest palettes, where the blue-green sits next to turquoise without repeating it. Smooth ovals and nuggets move fastest. Both take a bezel or a simple knotted line, and both look right against silver or brass. We list one strand of faceted pears at 7x15mm, small enough to hang as a single drop from an ear wire. A strong strand shows clear separation between pale sky and deep near-royal blue rather than one muddy tone. The lookalike is azurite-malachite, a carbonate: a drop of vinegar on a hidden spot fizzes there and does nothing here.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.care: Keep it to necklaces and earrings, where the beads stay clear of knocks. Wipe with a damp cloth and dry them. Skip the ultrasonic cleaner and anything acidic. Perfume and hairspray should go on before the strand does, so put the piece on last and take it off first.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.tagline: Copper blue locked in quartz, cut in Jaipur.
chrysocolla-and-shattuckite.judge: Draft B folds in more of the fact pack's concrete details (the vinegar test, the pear shape, the exact size) with sharper sensory specifics, while both handle lore as tradition with similar levels of embellishment. (a 35, b 38)

charoite.opening: Purple that moves. On the strand the color runs from pale lilac to deep violet, laid down in fibrous swirls that catch light and slide across the bead as you turn it, the way silk does. Black flecks of aegirine punctuate it. Sometimes a thread of orange tinaksite or a patch of white feldspar breaks in. Each oval reads as its own small map, and no two on a strand repeat. People reach for it because nothing else looks quite like it.
charoite.history: Charoite comes from one place on earth: the Murun massif in the Sakha Republic, Yakutia, in Russia. It takes its name from the Chara River, about 70 kilometers from where it was found, and was first described in 1978. When it turned up, some took it for a fake, the purple being hard to credit in a natural stone. The material formed roughly 120 million years ago, in potassic feldspar rocks at the contact of nepheline and aegirine syenites with limestone. Strictly speaking it is a rock rather than a single mineral, though the charoite mineral dominates it and gives the purple. That one valley in Siberia is still the only source, and the Russians control the supply. It works into cabochons, ornaments and beads, where the swirl has room to show. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen one strand at a time in Cupertino, California.
charoite.lore: The name traces to the Russian word chary, meaning charms or magic, a nod to the way the color and the shifting light struck the people who first handled it. Crystal tradition has since called it a stone of transformation, carried by people who believe it helps them meet change rather than resist it. People have long held that a stone worn close keeps such an idea near, and charoite gets worn that way, as a reminder more than an ornament. All of this is belief and tradition, not fact. It is what has gathered around a purple stone from one valley in the far north of Russia, in the decades since it was first named.
charoite.uses: We carry one strand of smooth ovals, 12 to 16 millimeters. Large is the point with this stone, since small beads chop the swirl into confetti and lose it. On a strong strand the silky band lifts clean off the surface as you tilt the bead, and the purple stays strong instead of getting crowded out by black and white. The ovals make a single-strand necklace on their own, or a focal run between plain silver spacers. Wire wrappers come to it, and so do designers building a purple palette and collectors who follow single-source stones.
charoite.care: Charoite sits at 5 to 6 on the Mohs scale, softer than quartz, so it scratches. Necklaces and earrings take daily wear well. Bracelets need more care, since wrists meet doorframes and desks. Wash with mild soap and lukewarm water, dry with a soft cloth, and keep it away from ultrasonic cleaners and heat.
charoite.tagline: One Siberian valley, and silk that moves when you turn it.
charoite.judge: Draft B renders the lore explicitly as belief with a clear disclaimer and paints more vivid, concrete imagery, though it adds a couple of small unsupported details (graduation, gemstone pairings) that cost it slightly on faithfulness. (a 37, b 40)

rhodochrosite.opening: Pink and cream in alternating bands, each one following the curve of the last. On a strand of large ovals the pattern shifts bead to bead: some cut across the rings like a sliced onion, others catch them lengthwise as soft stripes. Hold one to a window and the edges go translucent, the rose deepening toward raspberry where the band is thickest. Makers reach for it because no two beads repeat, and because that pink is a mineral color.
rhodochrosite.history: Rhodochrosite is manganese carbonate, and it turns up in only a small number of places where other manganese minerals are present. Notable occurrences include Cavnic in Romania and Butte, Montana, and Leadville, Colorado. The banded material used for beads comes from the Capillitas mine in Catamarca Province, Argentina, a locality worked by the Incas and long known for fine rhodochrosite stalactites. Those stalactites grew in old copper and silver workings, drip by drip, and the bands in a finished bead are their growth rings. The Argentine name, Inca Rose, stayed with the stone, which is now Argentina's national stone. Colorado's Sweet Home mine tells a different story: established as a silver mine in 1872 in the Alma Mining District at about 3,300 meters, it saw miners throw most of the rhodochrosite away, because it interfered with the amalgamation process then used for silver ore.
rhodochrosite.lore: In crystal tradition, rhodochrosite is called a stone of compassion, and the folklore around it stays in that register: kindness rather than power or luck. People who keep stones for their meanings group it with the pink stones for that reason. The Argentine name, Inca Rose, carries its own affection in the stories told about the Capillitas mine and the Incas who worked it, and Argentina has since made rhodochrosite its national stone, which gives the pink a second kind of meaning there. All of this is belief and custom rather than fact, passed along with the stone from one owner to the next.
rhodochrosite.uses: Banded rhodochrosite wants room to show its rings, so we favor smooth ovals in the 15 to 20mm range, one as the focal point of a necklace with plain metal or small pale beads on either side. Small rondelles lose the pattern entirely. Faceted hearts suit earrings and short pendants, where the pink reads clearly against silver. Kept in a pink palette, a single oval carries a whole necklace without competition. A stronger strand shows sharp, concentric rose to raspberry bands against cream, with light passing through at the bead edges; pale, mostly cream beads are the weaker end. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
rhodochrosite.care: This is a soft stone with easy cleavage, so keep it to necklaces and earrings rather than rings or bracelets. Perfume, sweat and anything acid will etch the surface. Wipe the beads with a damp cloth and dry them at once. No soaking, no ultrasonic cleaner, no heat.
rhodochrosite.tagline: Growth rings from an old silver mine, in rose and cream.
rhodochrosite.judge: Draft B pairs the required facts with more vivid, non-cliché sensory detail and keeps its added lore closer to the compassion tradition, while Draft A drifts into unsupported claims about romance and honest speech. (a 34, b 38)

pink-opal.opening: A strand of pink opal reads as one soft color from across a room. Up close it breaks into small differences: one bead a little deeper, the next carrying a cream swirl through its middle. The surface gives the light back in a waxy way rather than a glassy hit. There is no play of color in it, no flash of green or red. People reach for it because the pink is quiet and warm, closer to a garden petal than to candy.
pink-opal.history: Opal begins with water. Rain soaks into ground, carries dissolved silica down through rock, and in dry spells the water leaves solid silica behind in cracks and between the layers of sedimentary stone. Pink opal is the common kind: opal-CT mixed with the clay mineral palygorskite and a little chalcedony, slightly translucent to nearly opaque, its pink owed to organic compounds. It never shows play of color, which is the business of precious opal, the sort Australia became known for in the late 1800s. Peru supplies this stone, with the rough coming mainly from the Acari area of Arequipa, the same country that yields pastel blue and green common opal. It has long been sold as beads, cabochons and tumbled stones, and the best of it resembles pink coral while sitting harder on the scale, 5.5 to 6.5. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
pink-opal.lore: Opal carried weight in ancient Rome, where it stood for love and hope and where the name opalus was used as a word for precious stone in general. In 75 AD Pliny wrote of opali that carried such play within them that they matched the deepest colors a painter could mix, others seeming to hold burning sulphur or the blaze of oil. Later writers compared opals to volcanoes, galaxies and fireworks, and gave the great ones names like Pandora, Light of the World and Empress. Pink opal has a quieter reputation. Crystal tradition calls it a stone of emotional calm, something to steady the feelings of the person wearing it. That is tradition, not fact.
pink-opal.uses: This is a stone for soft palettes, and it goes where pink is meant to stay gentle: bridal work, spring pieces, gifts for a new baby. We cut it faceted, so the small flat planes pick up light without the surface turning glassy. Faceted ovals at 10x13mm hold the color evenly along a strand, and the 5mm size gives you that same pink at a smaller scale. Marquise reads longer than a round bead of similar weight. Gold fill sits well against the color. We list four strands at present, each chosen for even warm pink without gray. Cream mottling is normal.
pink-opal.care: Keep pink opal to earrings and necklaces. It is softer than rose quartz, so bracelets scuff it and rings are worse. The stone is porous. No ultrasonic cleaner, no perfume, no soaking, no heat. Put the piece on after scent and lotion, and store it away from anything harder.
pink-opal.tagline: Peruvian pink, no flash, cut in Jaipur.
pink-opal.judge: Draft B uses the fact pack's specific sizes, shapes, and strand count more precisely and avoids the duplication of Roman lore that Draft A repeats across two sections. (a 35, b 42)

dendrite-opal.opening: On the strand, the ground reads like paper: a soft, milky white with no fire in it, closer to porcelain than to glass. Across that white run thin black lines, branching the way frost climbs a window or a fern opens. Every bead carries a different drawing. Makers pick it up because the pattern does the work; you do not need a second focal stone, and the black and white sits quietly against skin and against metal.
dendrite-opal.history: Opal begins as silica dissolved in water, carried down into cracks and between rock layers, left behind as the water dries. Here the same seams gave manganese oxide room to creep outward in branching films, so the tree shapes are locked inside the white silica rather than drawn on its surface. Rough for these strands comes from Kazakhstan, Turkey, Mexico, and Madagascar. Opal itself has been in jewelry a very long time; the Romans called it opalus, a word that stood for precious stone, and in 75 AD Pliny wrote about the play of color inside it. Australian mines began producing commercially in the 1890s and became the main source. Dendrite opal is the Indian trade name for the white-and-black picture stone. The same picture in harder chalcedony is sold as dendritic agate, and some crystal shops in New Mexico call either one merlinite. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
dendrite-opal.lore: Opal has carried opposite reputations. In ancient Rome it stood for love and hope, and because it held the colors of other gems the Romans considered it the most precious and powerful of all. The Bedouins believed opals contained lightning and had fallen from the sky during thunderstorms. For centuries it was linked with royalty and good luck, until the novel Anne of Geierstein gave it a name for being unlucky, a superstition with nothing behind it. Opal is the October birthstone. In crystal tradition, stones with dendrites are tied to growth and steady patience, and people have long believed the branching pattern encourages things to take root. All of this is tradition rather than fact.
dendrite-opal.uses: The faceted dagger is the shape people ask for first, long enough to hold one whole dendrite from tip to shoulder, and it hangs well as a single pendant or in a graduated fringe. Smooth 12mm rounds make a plain knotted necklace that reads neutral with everything, and 5mm heishi gives you a flat black-and-white line for spacing or for a stacked bracelet. It suits minimalist and neutral-palette work, and it turns up often in wedding pieces. A stronger strand shows crisp, dark, well-separated branching on clean white rather than a gray haze. We keep nineteen strands listed.
dendrite-opal.care: Treat it as opal, not as quartz. At 5.5 to 6 on the Mohs scale it is softer than the stones it often sits beside, so keep it out of rings and away from heat and ultrasonic cleaners. Wipe with water and a soft cloth, and store it apart from harder beads.
dendrite-opal.tagline: Black ferns held in white opal, cut in Jaipur.
dendrite-opal.judge: Draft B grounds its uses and care sections in more concrete, fact-pack-matching specifics (strand count, bead sizes, Mohs range) while both drafts carry similar minor speculative additions. (a 36, b 39)

peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.opening: On the strand, the blue ovals read like pieces of a shallow sea. Pale sky in one bead, teal in the next. Each is smooth and slightly milky rather than glassy, and dark dendrites branch across some faces like ink pulled through paper. No two run the same way. The multi rondelles sit beside them in soft pink and green, with tan and blue mixed in, uneven on purpose. Color stays quiet here. The pattern does the talking.
peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.history: This is common opal from Peru. It comes from the same copper country deposits near Acari, in Arequipa, that give the market its pink opal. Copper is credited with the blue and green. The fine black and brown dendrites that wander through the better beads come from manganese oxide. Blue material from Peru carries the trade name Andean opal, and it turned up in Lima alongside chrysocolla in the early 1970s. Unlike precious opal, it has no play of color, so the appeal is the flat pastel body itself. Cutters have long worked it into cabochons and tumbled stones as well as beads. When a green Peruvian bead of this type went to the lab at the Gemological Institute of America, it came back identified as natural opal. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, then chosen strand by strand in Cupertino.
peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.lore: Opal has collected stories for a long time. In ancient Rome it stood for love and hope, and the Roman name opalus was used as a word for precious stone generally. In 75 AD Pliny wrote that some opals carried a play within them equal to the deepest and richest colors of painters. The Bedouins are said to have believed that opals held lightning and fell from the sky during thunderstorms. Much later the novel Anne of Geierstein gave the stone an unlucky reputation. Opal is the birthstone for October. In crystal tradition the pale blues are tied to calm speech, to saying the thing you mean without heat. All of it is belief and custom.
peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.uses: The blue smooth ovals we carry, 10 by 14 millimeters, are built for a focal spot. A full strand gives you enough of them to sort by pattern before you decide which faces sit forward. The multi rondelles, 5 to 7 millimeters, run in beachy and boho work, easy on their own or broken up with knotted cord. In blue, the strands worth holding out for are clean sky to teal with sharp, well defined dendrites, rather than the muddy gray green ones with heavy matrix. The multi should stay soft. Slightly uneven, bead to bead.
peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.care: Keep these beads out of ultrasonic cleaners. No household chemicals, no heat, no long soaking. At 5.5 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale they sit below quartz, which means grit and everyday knocks can mark a polished face. Handle them as the soft part of whatever you build.
peruvian-blue-opal-and-multi-peruvian-op.tagline: Pastel blue from copper country, dark manganese dendrites.

chrysoprase.opening: Strung together, chrysoprase settles into a clear apple green that seems to hold light. The best strands show a soft translucence and even color from bead to bead. Makers reach for it when a design needs freshness without glare. Gray patches and brown spots pull the eye. We carry smooth 8 mm rounds, 6 to 9 mm rondelles, and 10 to 18 mm ovals, cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand here in Cupertino.
chrysoprase.history: Chrysoprase is a variety of chalcedony colored apple green by traces of nickel. It measures about 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale. Among chalcedonies, it is second in value only to gem silica. The name comes from Greek words for golden apple or golden leek. It was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans and, in many periods since, has been worked into beads and cabochons; finer translucent material also takes clean facets. Geologically, it occurs as a secondary mineral in cavities and veins of serpentine, and notable deposits were recorded in California and Silesia. Much of the rough used for beads today comes from Queensland and Western Australia, as well as from Tanzania and Indonesia. The apple-green look is most prized when the color is even and there is a gentle glow through the stone.
chrysoprase.lore: In crystal tradition, chrysoprase is named the stone of optimism. People have long said its clear apple green brightens the outlook and invites a more positive frame of mind. Stories about the stone circulate in folklore and studio talk rather than science. The name comes from Greek words for golden apple or golden leek, and many connect that fruit-like color with hopefulness. So the story goes. These meanings are matters of tradition. Those who choose chrysoprase often do so for the way its color feels to them and for this long-standing reputation for optimism.
chrysoprase.uses: Designers reach for chrysoprase when a piece needs clear color with soft light. Color first. Rounds and rondelles sit close to the skin and read as a steady field of green, good for quiet necklaces and grounded bracelets. We keep smooth 8 mm rounds and 6 to 9 mm rondelles, with both smooth and faceted cuts depending on the feel you want. Ovals make strong focal notes. The pale "lemon" look is a different stone, nickel-bearing magnesite, and we tag it as magnesite.
chrysoprase.care: Keep chrysoprase away from prolonged heat or sunlight, which can fade the color. Store strands in the dark between uses and avoid ultrasonic cleaning. The light "lemon" material sold alongside it is nickel-bearing magnesite; it is softer, so use it in earrings and necklaces rather than rings.
chrysoprase.tagline: Apple-green chalcedony with a calm, even glow

carnelian.opening: Hold a strand of carnelian up to a window and the light comes through orange, sometimes closer to red, sometimes clouding pale where the color thinned as the stone grew. It is never one flat tone. The zoning drifts across a bead like weather crossing a field. This is chalcedony, colored by iron oxide, hard enough at 6.5 to 7 to hold a bright polish and take daily wear. Makers reach for it when a piece needs warmth.
carnelian.history: Carnelian is a variety of the silica mineral chalcedony, its orange to reddish brown coming from iron oxide dispersed through the stone. Gujarat, in western India, has cut carnelian for millennia, and rough and cut material also comes from Brazil, Uruguay, and Madagascar. Significant deposits are recorded at Yanacodo in Peru and Ratnapura in Sri Lanka, with material found as well in Indonesia, Iran, and Russia. The Greeks and Romans valued it for rings and signets, and some of their intaglios have kept a high polish better than stones harder than they are. A Sassanid seal from the third century carries a bull cut into carnelian. Where lapis lazuli came to be linked with priests, carnelian was the stone linked with kings. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
carnelian.lore: Ancient peoples across many regions favored this warm reddish stone, and the lore that grew around it gathered up health, luck, and royalty. Tradition makes carnelian a stone of courage. That is tradition, not fact, and worth saying plainly. Because the color sits so close to the color of blood, old healers were said to give it out as a general talisman, something kept near the skin rather than set out to be looked at. In crystal tradition it is still spoken of as a warm, steadying stone, one people reach for when they want to feel braver than they are. Belief again, and a long-lived one.
carnelian.uses: Carnelian sits easily in fall palettes, in boho and southwestern work, in men's bracelets, and on the workbenches of mala makers. We carry smooth pears at 10x14mm, cut to show the natural cloudy zoning, and faceted trilliants that catch small points of orange light along a collar. Two strands are listed online. The color runs warm beside brass and copper, and it holds its own next to matte black beads or plain sterling. A good strand reads translucent warm orange-red with soft banding, no two beads quite matched. Orange glass, by contrast, holds tiny bubbles.
carnelian.care: Carnelian is tough and takes ordinary wear well. Wash it in warm soapy water with a soft brush, then dry it before it goes back in the drawer. Keep it away from prolonged heat, so no sunny windowsills for weeks at a time and no leaving a bracelet on a hot dashboard.
carnelian.tagline: Orange light with cloud still in it.

blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.opening: Hold a strand of blue chalcedony to a window and the color seems to come from inside the bead rather than sit on it. Soft, cloudy, sometimes closer to gray or lilac than to sky. The blue is not pigment at all. It comes from light scattering off voids too small to see, which is why the surface reads as milk with a faint glow behind it. People reach for it when they want quiet color that still catches the eye across a room.
blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.history: Chalcedony is the compact, microcrystalline form of quartz, and it has been worked into ornament for a very long time. The name is thought to come from an ancient town at the Bosporus. Color in the chalcedony family traces back to metallic impurities present while the stone was forming, and material left as it came from the ground is often a grayish blue. Blue and lavender stone is generally named for where it is dug: Namibia, Turkey, Montana and Oregon all send out material in this family, and the depth of blue shifts from one source to the next. Because the color is delicate and the stone takes a high polish without fuss, gem carvers and jewelry designers have long favored it. Most pieces are cabbed or carved. Only rarely does a near-transparent piece get faceted. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.lore: Blue chalcedony appears in old lists of the stones set in the high priest's breastplate, the twelfth in Exodus 28:18 and 39:11, standing for the tribe of Benjamin. In the Greek and Latin texts it falls sixth, as it does in Ezekiel 28:13, and it comes first in Revelation 21:19. In crystal tradition it is known as the speaker's stone, a name that ties it to words and to being heard. That is belief and custom rather than fact, but it is part of why the stone keeps turning up in gifts between friends, and why people who talk for a living tend to like wearing it.
blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.uses: Smooth ovals do the most work here. Set a 10x14mm bead as the drop on a pendant and the cloudiness reads as depth instead of haze. Faceted pears around 9x15mm make good earrings, since the facets pick up light at the edges while the body of the bead stays soft. Rondelles move fastest, because they space larger stones without fighting them. On a stronger strand the inner glow is even from bead to bead, so the light seems to travel down the whole line. We carry smooth ovals, rondelles, nuggets and faceted pears, six strands listed at the moment.
blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.care: At 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale, blue chalcedony is a tough stone for how soft its color looks, hard enough for bracelets, which take more knocks than anything else you wear. The blue comes from structure rather than pigment, so what you see in a strand is what it stays.
blue-and-lavender-chalcedony.tagline: Cloudy blue with the light held inside it.

black-onyx-and-black-spinel.opening: On the tray, a strand of black onyx reads as one unbroken color, the facets catching light in small flat planes with no gray creeping in at the edges. Black spinel sits next to it and looks glassier, the light coming back harder off each facet, and the strand feels heavier in the hand than its size suggests. Makers reach for both when a piece needs a hard stop, a line of true dark against silver, brass, or pale stone.
black-onyx-and-black-spinel.history: Onyx is a chalcedony, itself a microcrystalline form of quartz, and in its banded black-and-white form it belongs to agate. Those straight, nearly parallel layers made it the great engraving stone of antiquity: carvers cut down through one band into the next to raise a pale figure against a dark ground. The Gemma Claudia, a Roman five-layer cameo of about the year 49 now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, shows how far that patience went. Solid black chalcedony, without banding, became the traditional black gemstone for jewelry. Black spinel is a different mineral entirely, magnesium aluminum oxide, and comes from Thailand, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka. Spinel's larger crystals from southeast Asian mines passed through the hands of kings and emperors, and for centuries red spinel wore the name ruby in Europe's crown jewels, among them the Black Prince's Ruby and the Timur Ruby. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand here in Cupertino, California.
black-onyx-and-black-spinel.lore: Few stones carry as much unhappy lore as onyx. Old writers tied it to quarrels, bad dreams, and gloom, and for centuries people looked for ways to counter those purported effects rather than set the stone aside, since they liked the look of it too much to give it up. Alongside that darker reading runs a steadier one: in crystal tradition both black onyx and black spinel are called protective, grounding stones, held to steady the wearer and turn away what is unwanted. It is said that a dark stone worn close keeps a person in their own footing. All of this is tradition and belief, not fact.
black-onyx-and-black-spinel.uses: Faceted marquise, daggers, and rondelles move fastest, and they suit different work. An 11mm rondelle strand strings straight into a plain necklace or spaces out a bracelet, and 10x40mm daggers make a fringe that hangs with real weight. Onyx anchors men's pieces and minimalist lines where one dark shape does all the talking. Spinel earns its place when you want natural black at fine-jewelry hardness, and it holds its own beside diamonds and gold. We keep fourteen onyx strands and six spinel, faceted and smooth, in marquise, pear, kite, tube, bar, and dagger from 15 to 45mm.
black-onyx-and-black-spinel.care: Both stones take daily wear without fuss, and both are safe in an ultrasonic cleaner. Keep onyx away from household cleaners and solvents. Warm water, mild soap, and a soft brush at the drill holes are enough. Store strands so the pointed shapes are not knocking against harder stones.
black-onyx-and-black-spinel.tagline: Two stones, one color, told apart by weight and light.

bumble-bee-jasper.opening: Hold a strand up and the color reads like a hive: lemon yellow beside apricot orange, split by black seams that run right through each bead. The bands are not surface markings. They cross the whole stone, so a faceted pear shows a different slice on every face. This is a soft rock, so facet edges come out gentle rather than knife sharp. Makers reach for it because nothing else on the bench is this loud, and the yellow is the sulfur itself.
bumble-bee-jasper.history: It comes from one small area of West Java, Indonesia: the southern slopes of the Mount Ciremai volcano, south of the town of Kuningan. The first material was reported as coming from Mount Papandayan, and that name still travels with the stone in the trade. Fritsch and Ivey published on the Ciremai source in 2018, following X-ray work by Attard and Petrov in 2017 on the orange bands. The trade calls it a jasper. It is not one. Jasper is a fine-grained quartz, hard and easy to live with; this is fibrous calcite grown in radiating fans around a fumarole, with native sulfur giving the yellow, the arsenic sulfides realgar and orpiment the orange, and pyrite with manganese oxides the black. Cutters took it up for the banding alone. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
bumble-bee-jasper.lore: In crystal tradition this is counted as a stone of nerve. Bright yellow stones have long been tied to the sun and to confidence, and this one is read the same way: it is said to help the wearer settle on a decision and act rather than circle it. The black bands are described as the counterweight, holding the yellow steady. Because the pattern recalls a bee, some tell it as a stone of industry and cooperation, of small steady work adding up over a season. Collectors keep it for a different reason, as a record of what a volcano leaves behind. All of it is belief carried alongside the stone, not fact.
bumble-bee-jasper.uses: Because the stone is soft, makers put it where it will not be knocked: statement earrings first, pendants second. A pair of faceted pears at 10 by 25mm hangs light enough to wear all day. The 10 by 40mm length reads as one long drop and wants almost nothing beside it. Marquise shapes give the banding its full width, and hearts suit one-off pendants. It sits well with warm metals and with plain black beads, which echo the dark seams. A stronger strand shows brighter lemon, more of it, and clean divisions between color and black instead of muddy edges. We sell it by the strand.
bumble-bee-jasper.care: Keep it to earrings and pendants, off the wrist. No soaking, no acids, no ultrasonic cleaner. Wipe with a dry or barely damp cloth and let it air. Store it apart from harder stones that can scratch the polish. Do not grind, sand or redrill a bead; work with it as it comes.
bumble-bee-jasper.tagline: Volcano yellow, black seams, cut for the ear.
