green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.opening: Green onyx comes up the strand as a row of small bottle-green windows. Translucent, even in color from bead to bead, the facets throwing light back in flat little planes. Green aventurine beside it is the quieter one. Opaque medium green, softer at the edges, with tiny flakes of mica that catch and let go as the strand turns. Makers reach for onyx when they want emerald color in a big shape. They reach for aventurine when they want green that reads like stone.
green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.history: Onyx proper is a banded variety of agate. It is a silicate mineral, and in proper usage the name describes the color pattern, light bands alternating with dark. Roman carvers cut it into cameos. One of them survives well: the Gemma Claudia, a five-layered onyx cameo made around the year 49, now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum. The name has traveled loosely ever since. It has been applied to parallel-banded alabaster and marble, and to calcite and obsidian and opal as well. Aventurine has a shorter record. It is quartzite crowded with fuchsite, a chromium-rich mica that gives both the green and the faint glitter, and much of the bead material is Indian. Its name comes from the Italian a ventura, by chance, after a copper-flecked glass first made by accident in Italy in the early 18th century. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India. We choose them one at a time in Cupertino, California.
green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.lore: Few stones carry as much gloom in old writing as onyx. The lore around it is full of negative associations. It has been linked with quarrels and with bad dreams, and people have long looked for ways to offset what they believed it carried. Worn in jewelry for millennia all the same. Green aventurine sits at the other end of that ledger. Tradition calls it the gambler's luck stone, and that is the name it still travels under in crystal folklore. Belief rather than fact. Still worth knowing when someone asks what the green is supposed to mean. The Italian root of the name says as much: by chance.
green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.uses: Green onyx earns its keep in statement shapes. Marquise and kite move fastest, since long facets stretch the color and it reads as emerald green from across a room. We stock marquise from 11x15mm up to 10x25mm. Pear too, when a softer outline suits the piece. A strong strand is even bottle green from bead to bead and clearly translucent held up to a window. Thirteen green onyx strands are online now. Green aventurine we carry in faceted pear and marquise, for lucky-green bracelets and men's malas. Those strands are not online yet.
green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.care: At 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale, both are fine for bracelets and daily wear. Wash in warm water with mild soap. Dry the beads and the thread all the way through. Keep them off harder stones in a shared pouch, and put jewelry on after lotion and scent rather than before.
green-onyx-and-green-aventurine.tagline: Two greens: one lit through, one flecked with mica.

pyrite.opening: Pyrite comes out of the tray looking like small machined parts. Brass-yellow, mirror-bright where two facets meet, throwing flat sparks rather than a glow. Lift a strand and the weight surprises you: pyrite runs about twice as heavy as chalcedony, so a bar strand hangs with the heft of a chain. Makers reach for it when a piece wants metal in it without another metal finding, and when they want that color to come from a stone.
pyrite.history: Pyrite is an iron sulfide, FeS2, and the most abundant sulfide mineral. Rough for beads comes mostly from Peru, out of the Huanzala district, and from China. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California. The name is Greek, from pyr, fire: struck against steel or another hard stone, pyrite throws sparks. Nodules have turned up in prehistoric burial mounds, which points to fire making. Wheel-lock guns spun a serrated wheel against a piece of pyrite before the flintlock, and flintlock firearms used it as spark-producing material as well. Dioscorides described it around 50 CE in his five books on medical materials. As a jewelry stone, faceted pyrite had a long run in the United States and Europe in the mid- to late-1800s, though most of it was sold then under the name marcasite.
pyrite.lore: The old nickname is fool's gold, given because to an untrained eye the color reads deceptively like a gold nugget. Crystal tradition leans on that resemblance and calls pyrite a money stone, kept in a cash drawer or worn to draw abundance. That is tradition, not fact. The older association is with fire itself. The Greek name says as much, and the nodules found in prehistoric burial mounds suggest people carried pyrite as a means of making fire, so it has long been a stone kept close by anyone who needed a spark. None of this is a promise. It is what has been believed about a heavy, metallic stone for a very long time.
pyrite.uses: Pyrite suits pieces that read industrial, and it does steady work in mixed-metal designs: the brass note comes from the stone rather than from another finding. Faceted bars in the longer lengths make a strong men's bracelet. A 10x25mm marquise holds a center position next to plainer beads and needs little around it. Heishi at 5mm is the quietest form, thin brass-yellow discs. On a stronger strand the flash is even and mirror-bright, facets crisp at the edges, with no dull brown patches. We list eight strands, all faceted, cut in Jaipur.
pyrite.care: Pyrite oxidizes slowly in humid air, so keep it dry. Store strands and finished pieces in a closed box with silica gel, and wipe the beads after wearing them. Never shower, swim or sleep in it. It is brittle for its hardness, which makes it a poor choice for rings.
pyrite.tagline: Brass-bright, heavy in the hand, happiest kept dry.

k2-granite.opening: White ground, blue dots. On a strand of K2 granite the beads read like small maps: chalky white rock salted with black grains, mica catching the light as you turn it, and round patches of azurite blue that look painted on. Some orbs are the size of a pinhead, some as wide as a fingernail, and they fade softly into the rock at their edges rather than stopping at a line. No two beads match. That is most of the appeal.
k2-granite.history: The material comes from the Skardu area of northern Pakistan, in the Karakoram, near the foot of the peak the Great Trigonometrical Survey of British India recorded as K2, the second peak measured in that range. Thomas Montgomerie made the first survey of the Karakoram, and the shorthand stuck to a mountain of 8,611 meters, second on Earth after Everest. The rock is granite: a light-colored igneous rock formed by slow crystallization of magma below the surface, here quartz, albite and minor mica, confirmed by x-ray diffraction. The blue arrived afterward. Azurite formed as a secondary oxidation product once the granite had solidified, seeping along grain boundaries into orbs a few millimeters to about two centimeters across. In the trade it goes by names it does not deserve, K2 Jasper and raindrop azurite. It is granite, and our tags say so. Our strands are cut in Jaipur, India, and chosen strand by strand in Cupertino, California.
k2-granite.lore: Tradition calls K2 a stone of balance. That is the whole of the claim as it reaches us, repeated in crystal circles without much elaboration, and we pass it along the same way: belief, not fact. People who keep the beads speak of balance in their own terms, and the word has stayed attached to a rock that holds two unlike things in one piece. Nothing in it is a promise, and none of it takes the place of anything else. If the idea appeals to you, hold it the way traditions are best held: loosely, and without asking it to do work.
k2-granite.uses: This one goes into men's and unisex lines and onto the workbenches of designers who like plain metal and rough texture. A faceted marquise at 15 by 45mm hangs well from a heavy chain or a leather cord. Rectangles at 11 by 15mm sit between darker stones as spacers, and pyramids give a shoulder of white to catch light beside the blue. Since no two beads carry their orbs the same way, sorting a strand before you set it is worth the time. A stronger strand has a clean white ground with several saturated blue orbs on each bead and mica that glints as you tilt it. We list twelve strands.
k2-granite.care: Keep it in necklaces and earrings. The feldspar in the granite scratches and dulls in bracelets, where beads knock against a desk all day. Wash in warm soapy water with a soft brush and dry it well. Keep acids away from it, including household cleaners, since they attack the blue azurite.
k2-granite.tagline: Granite from the foot of K2, with azurite raindrops.

ruby-zoisite.opening: Green first, the flat opaque green of a painted shutter. Then the red comes through in patches, sometimes a wide bloom, sometimes a scatter of pink, with black flecks of hornblende sitting between. Run a fingernail along a faceted marquise and you feel a shallow groove where the soft zoisite meets the hard ruby. The ruby stands proud. Makers reach for it because it carries three colors at once and needs nothing else beside it.
ruby-zoisite.history: Zoisite got its name from a collector named Zois, after the first find in the Sau-Alp mountains of Austria in 1805, when it was called saualpite. The rock that makes these beads comes from much farther south. In the Longido district of Tanzania, in the Arusha Region, ruby was found about a hundred years ago, making it one of the longest-known occurrences in Africa. The material from the Mundarara mine is large red corundum crystals grown into a chrome-green zoisite matrix, speckled with black amphibole. Most of it has always gone to carvers, who make sculptures and ornamental objects, since the ruby is opaque rather than facet grade. Now and then clear crystals turn up: a GIA team collected sixteen transparent rubies there in July 2016. Local names stuck too. Anyolite comes from the Maasai word anyoli, green, and the rock has also been sold as Tanganyika artstone.
ruby-zoisite.lore: Few stones carry as much lore as ruby. Across centuries and many cultures, the red corundum was tied to myth and romance, and some of that follows it here even though the red in these beads is opaque and set in rock. In crystal tradition, ruby zoisite is a stone of vitality, the green and the red held to work together rather than apart. People who work with it speak of it in those terms, and that is part of why the stone gets picked up off the table. All of this is belief and custom rather than fact, and worth holding lightly.
ruby-zoisite.uses: Marquise and daggers move fastest. A 10x25mm marquise hangs well as a fringe or a single drop, and daggers give a row of points along a collar without much weight. Pears take a bail cleanly for earrings. Holiday designers use it for red and green without going literal, watermelon-palette makers like the pink and green together, and men's lines use it when they want color that is not shiny. We list twenty strands, faceted and organic cut, from 10x15mm shapes up to long drops. They are cut in Jaipur and chosen here in Cupertino, with an eye for beads that show all three colors: green, red, and a little black. Weaker strands are mostly green with pink specks.
ruby-zoisite.care: Sturdy enough for necklaces and earrings; bracelets take more care, since the zoisite is softer than the ruby and knocks against door frames and desks. Wash in warm soapy water with a soft brush and dry the knots. Keep faceted pieces out of the ultrasonic.
ruby-zoisite.tagline: Green rock, red crystal, black flecks between.

freshwater-cultured-pearl.opening: Hold a strand of fireballs up to a window and the light comes back in a hard, narrow line. Each pearl has a round body with a tail pulled out like a flame, no two tails the same. The color reads white, with a blush of pink or mauve that shifts as the strand turns. The rounds next to them are quieter and even. Makers reach for both because nacre answers skin better than it answers a lamp.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.history: A pearl is nacre, mostly aragonite with conchiolin, laid down in layers by a mollusk. In fresh water the work is done by mussels, and today China is effectively the only commercial producer, with Japan and the United States farming on a limited scale. The idea has a long history in China, where workers were producing freshwater blister pearls in the 13th century by opening a mussel's shell, setting in small pellets of mud or small bosses of wood, bone or metal, and returning the animal to its bed for about three years. Japanese freshwater cultivation began in 1935, and Masao Fujita worked at Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture with the Biwa pearly mussel, Hyriopsis schlegelii. Lake Biwa supplied pearls in many colors until 1982, and from 1962 some farms moved to Lake Kasumigaura in Ibaraki Prefecture. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires that farmed freshwater pearls be sold as freshwater cultured pearls.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.lore: Tradition calls pearls tears of the moon. That is the whole of it: an image, handed on as tradition rather than fact, that has followed pearls from one telling to the next. The comparison is easy to see on a fireball strand, where the white body carries a pink or mauve cast and the tail takes light in a thin line. Nothing in the phrase explains how a pearl forms; a mussel does that, layer by layer, in fresh water. Still, people repeat it, and it changes how a strand feels in the hand. We pass the phrase along as tradition and leave it there.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.uses: We carry two kinds, chosen strand by strand in Cupertino: baroque fireballs from 15 to 25mm and rounds from 8 to 10mm, white with a pink or mauve overtone. A fireball is large enough that one on a chain is a finished pendant, which is how most people use them. Rounds suit bridal work, classic single strands and layering necklaces. Luster is the thing to look at: sharp, clear reflections mean thick nacre, while a soft, fuzzy surface means less of it. On fireballs, look for a blemish-light body and a tail that reads metallic. On rounds, look for matched size and few pits.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.care: Pearls are soft, between 2.5 and 4.5 on the Mohs scale, and nacre dislikes chemistry. Last on, first off. Keep perfume, hairspray and anything acidic away from the strand, and never put pearls in an ultrasonic cleaner. Wipe them with a damp cloth after wearing and let them dry before storing.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.tagline: Grown in a mussel, judged by the light it returns.
freshwater-cultured-pearl.judge: Draft B sticks closer to the fact pack's exact figures and explicitly preserves the 'tradition, not fact' framing, while reading in plainer, less adjective-heavy prose. (a 33, b 39)

multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.opening: A strand of these lies flat in the palm like a stack of small coins, discs of four and five millimeters set on edge. Carnelian orange, then pale chalcedony, then the apple green of chrysoprase, then amethyst, then moonstone that shifts blue when you tilt it, then a bead of opal. The plan repeats down the string. Makers reach for them because one strand carries a whole palette, and a bracelet can be strung and knotted in an afternoon.
multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.history: Heishi, pronounced hee shee, means shell bead in the Eastern Keresan language of the Santo Domingo Indians. The beads themselves are small discs and tubes, made of shell or of ground and polished stone, and they come from the Kewa Pueblo people of New Mexico, formerly Santo Domingo Pueblo, who worked them before that people used metal in jewelry. The oldest known specimens go back to around 6000 BCE, though the same technique of grinding and polishing was used in northern Africa some thirty thousand years earlier, with ostrich eggshell. Modern heishi is commonly mass-produced by machine. Our strands come from Jaipur, where cutting rooms keep the remainders from larger orders and string them into mixes, and we choose them strand by strand here in Cupertino.
multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.lore: There is an old idea, passed along as tradition rather than fact, that wearing many stones together spreads their luck around, so that no single bead carries the whole weight. Whatever you make of that, the habit of mixing is old and widespread. Traditional Tibetan necklaces set dzi beads among coral, and sometimes amber and turquoise as well, and the dzi have long been prized as protective amulets, held to bring the wearer spiritual benefit. In Ghana and across West Africa, aggry glass beads were strung into necklaces and bracelets in much the same spirit, several kinds worn as one. A mixed strand sits in that long line.
multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.uses: The 4 to 5mm heishi is the workhorse. Strung on cord it makes a flat, flexible bracelet that sits close to the wrist, and one strand covers the whole piece without any planning of color. Beginners and bracelet makers like it for exactly that, and kit sellers buy heishi by the strand and split it. The large tyre mixes bring in lapis, amazonite, pink opal, and sunstone, in fewer and heavier beads. Look for a repeating color plan, even sizing, and no filler padding out the count. The tag lists every stone, and it is worth reading species by species rather than going by color.
multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.care: A mixed strand is only as tough as its softest bead, and here that is opal, around 5.5 to 6 on the Mohs scale. Keep these away from ultrasonic cleaners, household chemicals, and long soaks. Wipe them with a soft dry cloth, and store them where harder beads cannot rub against them.
multi-gemstone-heishi-and-designer-mix-s.tagline: A whole palette on one string, cut in Jaipur.

ruby.opening: Held to a window, a ruby strand reads as a run of small red lamps. Some beads go deep, nearly brown. Others sit closer to raspberry. The color is uneven from one bead to the next, and that shading is much of the character. Faceted rondelles at 2.5mm catch light in short flashes rather than long ones, and teardrops hang point down with the color pooling at the wide end. People reach for them when they want real red corundum at a working price.
ruby.history: Ruby is red corundum: aluminum oxide with chromium sitting in the crystal structure. More chromium, stronger red. The name comes from ruber, Latin for red. In Sanskrit the stone is ratnaraj, king of precious stones, and it is mentioned four times in the Bible, tied there to beauty and wisdom. It sits among the traditional cardinal gems, along with amethyst and sapphire. Asia supplied gem corundum for more than a thousand years, and Myanmar still carries weight in the bead trade, as does India. Africa came forward later. Mozambique and Madagascar are now steady sources for material that gets cut into beads. Our strands are cut in Jaipur and chosen one strand at a time here in Cupertino, California.
ruby.lore: Early cultures set ruby beside the red of blood in the veins and believed the stone held the power of life itself. Many cultures have long called it a king's gem. The folklore clusters on power and protection. Wealth comes into it as well. Owning one was said to benefit the holder's estates and to help wealth gather. Red has long stood for the strongest feelings, love and anger alike, and tradition ties ruby to passion above all else. These are old beliefs, carried along with the stone rather than proven by it. Ruby is the July birthstone. It is also the gem given for the fifteenth and fortieth wedding anniversaries.
ruby.uses: Two shapes do most of the work here. Faceted rondelles from 2.5 to 3mm make good spacers, a few between gold fill rounds or flanking a larger center bead, and they suit a plain line bracelet where the shading reads as one long gradient. Pear and teardrop drops in the 4.5 to 5mm range make earrings that need nothing added. We list four strands, sold by the 8 inch and by the 16, with roughly 8 to 15 carats per 8 inches. Stronger flash shows as sharp separate points of light off the facets rather than a soft general glow.
ruby.care: Ruby is 9 on the Mohs scale and takes daily wear well. Chemistry is another matter. Lemon juice and jewelry dip both etch the surface, and a torch will do worse, so keep flame away from a strung strand. Wipe with a soft dry cloth. Store the beads where harder stones cannot rub the drill holes.
ruby.tagline: Red corundum cut small, shaded bead to bead.
